title: CoLES: Contrastive Learning for Event Sequences with Self-Supervision (Babaev et al., SIGMOD 2022, arXiv 2002.08232v3)
topics: 1 Introduction: embeddings for event sequences; why BERT/CPC-style context prediction does not fit interleaved financial streams; contributions
2 Related work: contrastive learning (Hadsell 2006, FaceNet, SimCLR), surrogate classes, CPC, recommender self-supervision (Cloze, auxiliary seq2seq), item-ID sequences vs multi-field events
3.1 Problem formulation: entity = latent stochastic process, one observed realisation, no positive pairs; Phase 1 self-supervised, Phase 2a embeddings as features, Phase 2b fine-tuning (Fig 1)
3.2 Random slices sampling as augmentation (Algorithm 1), bootstrap analogy, periodicity/repeatability assumption
3.3 Training: batch of N sequences x K slices, positives = same sequence, negatives = different; Hadsell contrastive loss; negative sampling; unit-norm embeddings so d^2 = 2 - 2 c_u.c_v
3.4 Encoder: event encoder phi_evt (embeddings for categoricals, batch norm for numericals, concatenated) + sequence encoder phi_seq (GRU), last state is the embedding
4.0 Datasets (age group, churn, assessment, retail age, scoring), repeatability check via KL (Fig 2), split protocol, training speed, hyperparameters (Table 1)
4.1 Baselines: LightGBM, hand-crafted aggregate features, self-supervised baselines NSP, SOP, RTD, CPC
4.2.1 Design choices: slice strategy (Table 2), loss functions (Table 4), negative sampling (Table 5), encoder type (Table 3), embedding size (Fig 3)
4.2.2 Self-supervised embeddings as frozen features (Table 6)
4.2.3 Fine-tuned embeddings (Table 7)
4.2.4 Semi-supervised: label-fraction curves (Fig 4)
4.3 Commercial settings: legal-entity and retail embeddings at a large European financial company (Tables 8-11), including fraudulent money transfer monitoring
4.3.1 Deployment: training vs inference, Hadoop horizontal scaling, incremental GRU updates, quantization of embeddings
5 Conclusions
key_results: Sec 3.1: Core idea. Each entity is a latent class/stochastic process; only one finite sequence per entity is observed, so there are no ready-made positive pairs. Embedding M(x_e)=c_e in R^d should place sub-sequences of the same entity close and different entities far.

Sec 3.2 Algorithm 1 (random slices): hyperparameters m, M (min/max slice length), k (number of slices). For each of k: draw length T_i uniform in [1,T]; keep only if T_i in [m,M]; draw start s uniform in [0,T-T_i); take contiguous slice. Discard too short/long rather than clip.

Sec 3.2 assumption: lifetime event sequences are periodic/repeatable, so slices of one sequence resemble each other more than slices of other sequences. Supported empirically by Fig 2 (KL between event-type distributions of same-client slices much smaller than different-client slices; text posts show no such gap).
Sec 3.3 Batch: N sequences x K slices each; same-sequence pairs positive, cross-sequence pairs negative.
Sec 3.3 Loss: L_uv = 1/2 Y_uv d(u,v)^2 + 1/2 (1-Y_uv) max{0, rho - d(u,v)}^2 (Hadsell 2006), Euclidean d; negative term prevents collapse. Margin rho=0.5 in Table 4.
Sec 3.3: embeddings restricted to unit norm so squared distance = 2 - 2 c_u^T c_v, needing only pairwise dot products; makes distance-aware negative sampling cheap.

Sec 3.4: encoder M = phi_seq({phi_evt(x_t)}); event encoder concatenates per-categorical embeddings and batch-normed numericals; GRU sequence encoder with learnt c_0; c_t+1 = GRU(z_t+1, c_t); last c_T is the sequence embedding.
Table 2: random slices beat random samples (non-contiguous) and random disjoint segments on all 4 datasets (e.g. Assess 0.618 vs 0.563; Retail 0.542 vs 0.523/0.505).
Table 3: encoder type matters little (LSTM/GRU similar); transformer worse on Churn (0.780 AUROC vs 0.812-0.823), Assess (0.542 vs ~0.62) and Retail.

Table 4: classic contrastive loss with margin 0.5 matches or beats binomial deviance, histogram, margin, triplet losses; authors speculate better contrastive-task performance does not always mean better downstream performance.
Table 5: hard negative mining beats random negative sampling (Age 0.639 vs 0.626, Assess 0.618 vs 0.593); distance-weighted in between.
Fig 3: downstream quality saturates with embedding size (bias-variance reading); training time and memory scale linearly with size.

Table 6 (frozen CoLES embeddings into LightGBM, 5 runs): CoLES best on Churn AUROC 0.843 vs hand-crafted 0.825; on par on Age 0.638 vs 0.631, Assess 0.601 vs 0.602, Scoring 0.792 vs 0.779; hand-crafted slightly better on Retail (0.547 vs 0.539). CPC and RTD also beat hand-crafted on Scoring (0.791); SOP/NSP baselines weak.
Table 7 (fine-tuned): CoLES pretrain is best on all four public tasks (Age 0.644, Churn 0.827, Assess 0.615, Retail 0.552) vs supervised-only (0.628, 0.817, 0.602, 0.542).
Fig 4 / Sec 4.2.4: CoLES gain over supervised-only grows as labeled fraction shrinks; CoLES fine-tuning consistently above CPC at all label volumes.

Table 10 (legal entities, AUROC; baseline / CoLES / baseline+CoLES): insurance leads 0.71/0.85/0.85; credit leads 0.75/0.79/0.79; credit scoring 0.73/0.71/0.77; holding structure 0.92/0.97/0.97; fraudulent money transfer monitoring 0.82/0.84/0.85.
Table 11 (retail, AUROC): retail credit scoring 0.88/0.87/0.92; churn 0.74/0.65/0.76; insurance leads 0.75/0.74/0.78. Hybrid hand-crafted + CoLES is best or tied everywhere.
Sec 4.3: legal entities gain more than individuals because grouping keys for hand-crafted aggregates are unclear for fund transfers (sender/receiver), so CoLES learns the aggregation level itself.

Sec 4.3.1 deployment: encoder trained on a subset (10M corporate, 5M retail clients), applied to >90M cards; no distributed training; inference horizontally scaled on Hadoop; GRU enables incremental embedding updates c_t+k from c_t as new transactions arrive; quantizing floats to 0-15 shrinks a 256-d embedding from 1Kb to 128 bytes.
Abstract claim: deployment yields financial gains of hundreds of millions of dollars per year (no breakdown given).

gems: Algorithm 1 is tiny and exactly implementable: random contiguous slices with length filter [m,M]; the whole augmentation is 'bootstrap for a single long sequence' (Sec 3.2). Table 1 gives per-dataset m, M, k=5, batch N (64-256), embedding size (100-1024), lr, epochs.
Fig 2 KL test: a cheap diagnostic to check whether your data suits CoLES (same-user slice KL vs different-user slice KL), with a negative control from text posts (Fig 2d).
Unit-norm trick: squared Euclidean distance becomes 2 - 2 c_u.c_v, so the whole batch loss is a similarity matrix (Sec 3.3).
Batch size arithmetic in Sec 4.0.4: 64 individuals x 5 slices = 320 sub-sequences x ~90 transactions ~ 28,800 transactions per batch, 142 ms on one Tesla P-100.
Why hand-crafted features fail for legal entities (Sec 4.3): no natural group-by key for sender/receiver, CoLES learns the aggregation; contrast with MCC group-by for cards.
Fraud-relevant result: fraudulent money transfer monitoring AUROC 0.82 baseline, 0.84 CoLES alone, 0.85 hybrid (Table 10): a modest, honest gain that illustrates complement-not-replace.
Churn on retail: CoLES alone 0.65 vs baseline 0.74 but hybrid 0.76 (Table 11) - embeddings can lose alone yet add on top of features.
Quantization: 256-d float embedding 1Kb -> 128 bytes using 4-bit buckets with little loss (Sec 4.3.1).
Incremental inference with GRU vs transformers: new transactions update the stored embedding without reprocessing history (Sec 4.3.1), a concrete production argument for recurrent encoders.
Dataset scale list: scoring set 443M card transactions, 1.47M persons, 2.76% default rate (Sec 4.0.1).

pedagogy: Short applied-ML conference paper (11 pages, SIGMOD 2022 data-management track). No theorems or proofs; method presented as one algorithm box, one loss formula, one architecture paragraph, then ablation tables on four public datasets (age group, churn, game assessment, retail age) plus a scoring set, then in-house bank results. Evidence style is empirical comparison against hand-crafted-feature LightGBM and adapted NSP/SOP/RTD/CPC baselines, with 5-fold CV for ablations and mean+/-std over 5 runs for headline tables. Strongly oriented toward practitioners: hyperparameter table, training speed, deployment and storage notes. Prerequisites: embeddings, metric learning/contrastive loss, GRU/LSTM, gradient boosting, AUROC/accuracy. No exercises. Caveats worth teaching: the fraud result is an internal bank task reported only as AUROC with no dataset released and no precision/recall or cost detail; the $100M+ claim is unsubstantiated; public benchmarks are not fraud tasks (age, churn, assessment, retail, default scoring); datasets are user-level labeled so slices of one user share a label. Code for public experiments: github.com/dllllb/coles-paper.

title: Towards a Foundation Purchasing Model: Pretrained Generative Autoregression on Transaction Sequences (NPPR) — Skalski, Sutton, Burrell, Perez, Wong (Featurespace), ICAIF '23, arXiv:2401.01641v2
topics: Abstract: generative pretraining for transaction embeddings; 180 issuers, 5.1B transactions, card-fraud VDR gain on hold-out issuers
1 Introduction: foundation models, hand-engineered-feature pain, four contributions (NPPR method, public benchmarks, fraud at scale, MCC semantics)

2 Related work: autoregressive LM / MLM / NSP / replaced-token detection; contrastive (SimCLR, SAINT, SimCSE, CPC, CoLES); non-contrastive (BYOL, Barlow Twins, SwAV, SimSiam); graph methods (GraphSage, LaundroGraph) and why they are batch/AML rather than real-time

3 Generative modelling on transaction sequences: 3.1 NPPR method (next event prediction NP, past reconstruction PR, Eq.1-3, Fig.1); 3.2 Architecture (MLP -> GRU -> projection; decoders as MLP heads; why GRU over transformer for production latency)

4 Experiments on public datasets: 4.1 Datasets (Rosbank churn, SberBank age, X5 expenditure, AlphaBank credit default; Table 1); 4.2 Hyperparameters; 4.3 Baselines (hand-engineered aggregates, SimCSE, RED/RTD, CoLES); 4.4 Results: 4.4.1 vs baselines (Table 2), 4.4.2 ablation NP vs PR (Table 3), 4.4.3 averaging vs last embedding (Table 4)

5 Application to fraud detection at scale: 5.1 Pretrained embedding model; 5.2 Fraud models (datasets, baseline Jha et al. 14 aggregates, MLP models, VDR @ FP-ratio metric); 5.3 Quantitative results (Fig.2); 5.4 Visualising the embedding space (MCC t-SNE Fig.3, nearest neighbours Table 5)
6 Conclusions: foundation-model homogenisation; future work on privacy, bias, few-shot
References
key_results: NPPR objective (Sec 3.1): per-event loss L_e = sum_t [(1-alpha) L_NP_t + alpha L_PR_t]. NP (Eq.1): decoder predicts next event's features from embedding e_t; per-feature loss MSE for numeric, cross-entropy for categorical, summed over features. PR (Eq.2): decoder gets e_t and time gap delta to a past event x_{t-k} and reconstructs it; weights w=exp(-delta/lambda) decay with time gap, at most K past events. Encoder E: e_t = E(x_t,...,x_0).

Architecture (3.2): per-feature preprocessing (normalised numerics, embedding layer for categoricals, time-gap-to-previous-event feature) -> concat -> MLP -> GRU -> projection to embedding. GRU chosen because in production only hidden state + new event need be stored/processed (low-latency real-time decisioning); decoders are simple MLPs with softmax heads for categoricals.

Public benchmarks (Table 2, frozen embeddings into MLP): NPPR beats hand-engineered features, SimCSE, RED/RTD and CoLES on all 4 tasks. FeatEng/SimCSE/RTD/CoLES/NPPR: Churn AUC 0.798/0.650/0.827/0.813/0.845; Age acc 0.626/0.410/0.590/0.633/0.642; Expnd MSLE 0.743/1.140/0.747/0.758/0.723; Default AUC 0.768/0.630/0.765/0.765/0.798. Hand-engineered features were the strongest baseline on several tasks (beat CoLES on 2 datasets, RTD on 3, SimCSE on all).

Ablation (Table 3): both tasks together beat either alone on all datasets. NPPR vs PR vs NP: Churn 0.845/0.833/0.814; Age 0.642/0.542/0.630; Expnd 0.723/0.747/0.733; Default 0.798/0.744/0.795. NP alone beats other baselines on 3 of 4 problems; PR alone beats NP on churn (hypothesis: reaches further back, captures decline in transaction velocity). Tuned alpha: 0.1 churn, 0.001 age, 0.005 expenditure, 0.001 default; lambda = 2 months.

Averaging vs last-event embedding (Table 4): averaging all event embeddings changes NPPR by -0.5% churn, +6.1% age, -0.3% MSLE expnd (better), +0.6% default; CoLES -1.0%, +0.3%, 0.0%, -1.8%. Averaging helps static-attribute tasks (age), can hurt churn (oversmooths recent decline); does not help CoLES because its embeddings are already similar across an entity's events.

Fraud at scale (Sec 5): one embedding model pretrained on 180 European issuers (ISO 8583), >5.1B transactions, 12 months, 61M cardholders; MLP 2x2048 -> GRU 1024 -> 768-d embedding, lambda 2 months, alpha 0.001. Evaluated on 3 hold-out issuers in different countries (11 months; 17M, 3.5M, 1.8M cardholders; fraud rates 0.04%, 0.027%, 0.11%), split temporally AND by cardholder; genuine transactions downsampled for classifier training, not for pretraining.

Baseline = Jha et al. 2012: primary transaction attributes + 14 hand-engineered aggregation features over past windows; classifier = 3x1024 MLP, lr 1e-3, batch 1024, dropout 0.2, early stopping. Adding NPPR embeddings improves VDR at all FP-ratios on all three issuers; up to 140% uplift at 5:1 FP-ratio; pretrained-only embeddings are comparable to embeddings self-supervised-finetuned on the target issuer (transfer to out-of-domain data).

Metric definition (5.2.4): VDR = value-weighted true positive rate; FP-ratio = false positives / true positives; threshold tuned to FP-ratio between 1:1 and 20:1. Rationale: false positives decline genuine transactions, costing issuer and cardholder experience; production fraud systems judged at high-precision operating points.

Embedding interpretability (5.4): MCC embedding = mean of transaction embeddings for that MCC; nearest neighbours cluster by industry with no MCC side-information given (Table 5: Lufthansa -> British Airways 0.23, Scandinavian Airlines 0.32, Air France 0.33, Swissair 0.35, Turkish Airlines 0.38; Hilton -> Doubletree 0.19, Hampton Inns 0.20, Fairmont 0.28, Penta 0.29, Marriott 0.32; Fast Food -> Eating places 0.14, Convenience stores 0.26, Bakeries 0.27, News Dealers 0.30, Drug Stores 0.35). Hotel and airline clusters sit close (correlated purchases). Analogy to word-embedding semantics.

Positioning claims: generative (autoregressive) SSL suits tasks predicting future behaviour (churn, expenditure, default); contrastive CoLES is competitive for static attributes; graph methods are batch/AML, not real-time fraud.

Sec 4.4.2: past-reconstruction alone beats next-event prediction on churn (0.833 vs 0.814 AUC) because churn is a decline in transaction velocity that needs long-range memory — a clean mechanism story for why an auxiliary loss helps.
Sec 4.4.3 / Table 4: averaging the sequence embedding gives +6.1% on age but -0.5% on churn — pooling choice depends on whether the target is a static trait or recent change.

Sec 4.3/Table 2: hand-engineered aggregates are a strong baseline: they beat SimCSE everywhere and CoLES on two datasets; SimCSE with dropout-only augmentation is terrible on transactions (age accuracy 0.410).

Sec 5.2.1: fraud rates of 0.04%, 0.027%, 0.11% with temporal AND entity-level splits and downsampling of genuine transactions only for classifier training, not pretraining — concrete leakage/imbalance hygiene.
Sec 3.2: GRU over transformer justified by serving constraints — constant-state per event, important under real-time decisioning latency.

title: Tabular Transformers for Modeling Multivariate Time Series (TabBERT, TabGPT), Padhi et al., arXiv 2011.01843v2
topics: Abstract: tabular time series, quantization as the language metaphor, TabBERT and TabGPT
1 Introduction: static vs dynamic tabular data; related work (TabNet, TaPas, TaBERT; GAN/VAE synthetic tabular generation); contributions
2 TabBERT: unsupervised learning of multivariate time series representation
2.1 From language modeling to tabular time series (Fig 1; quantize continuous fields, per-field local vocabulary, sample = window of rows)
2.2 Hierarchical Tabular BERT (Fig 2; field transformer per row -> row embedding -> sequence transformer; MLM with field-level masking)
2.3 TabBERT features for classification: synthetic card transaction dataset, TabBERT training setup, fraud detection task, Table 1
2.4 TabBERT features for regression: Beijing PM2.5 pollution dataset, Table 1
3 TabGPT: generative modeling of tabular time series (Fig 3; per-user GPT, SEP token; field histogram chi2 evaluation Fig 4; FID on TabBERT embeddings, Eq 2, Table 2)
4 Conclusion
5 References
key_results: Quantization of continuous fields so every field has its own finite local vocabulary; this is what makes language-model machinery applicable to tabular rows (Sec 1, 2.1, Conclusion).
Sample definition: window t=[t_{i+1},...,t_{i+T}] of T consecutive rows with a stride (Eq 1, Sec 2.1-2.2).

Hierarchical TabBERT: field-level transformer encodes each row (intra-transaction, local relationships) into a row embedding; these are fed as tokens to a second sequence-level BERT (inter-transaction, global/temporal) (Sec 2.2, Fig 2). Hierarchical transformers borrowed from NLP document models (HIBERT etc.).

Pre-training: masked language modeling on fields, mask 15% of fields with [MASK], cross-entropy to recover the original field token; the label column isFraud? is excluded from pre-training to avoid biasing representation (Sec 2.3).
Downstream protocol: TabBERT frozen, MLP or LSTM head on pooled row-level embeddings; baseline is same head on raw embedded features (Sec 2.3).

Table 1 results: Fraud F1 raw MLP 0.74, raw LSTM 0.83, TabBERT MLP 0.76, TabBERT LSTM 0.86; PRSA pollution RMSE raw MLP 38.5, raw LSTM 43.3, TabBERT MLP 34.2, TabBERT LSTM 32.8. Gain on fraud is modest for MLP (+0.02) and +0.03 for LSTM.
Fraud setup: 10 contiguous rows, stride 10, per user; 2.4M samples, 29,342 fraudulent; fraud class upsampled to roughly equalize classes in training; F1 on a 480K-sample test set (Sec 2.3).

TabFormer synthetic dataset: rule-based generator with stochastic sampling (after Altman 2019), 24M transactions, 20,000 users, 12 fields mixing continuous and discrete nominal (merchant name, address, amount...); released open source (Sec 2.3).

TabGPT: non-hierarchical; transactions concatenated with [SEP] and fed directly to a GPT causal decoder; one model per user, trained on 10-transaction chronological segments; generation conditioned on the first transaction of each group of ten, predicting the other nine (Sec 3, Fig 3). Two users with ~60k transactions each.

Fidelity evaluation, two levels: per-field histograms compared by chi-square distance chi2(X,X') = 1/2 sum (x_i - x'_i)^2/(x_i + x'_i) (aggregate, Fig 4, entropy bars vs chi2 line); and sequence-level Frechet distance FID = ||mu_a-mu_b||^2 + Tr(S_a+S_b-2(S_a S_b)^{1/2}) on TabBERT mean-pooled sequence embeddings, inspired by FID/FD (Eq 2, Sec 3).

Table 2 FID: real user1 vs real user2 = 492.92; GPT-Gen user1 vs real user1 22.90, vs real user2 497.68; GPT-Gen user2 vs real user1 515.94, vs real user2 49.08 - generated data matches its own user and preserves cross-user distance.

Claim of novelty: first work to address tabular time series with transformers (Sec 1). Caveats visible in the text: single synthetic fraud set with rule-based labels, only two users for generation, no comparison to GBDT on engineered features, only 4-page treatment.

The 'language metaphor': a transaction is a sentence of field-words each with its own vocabulary; a user history is a document; quantizing Amount is the key enabling step.
Honest effect size: TabBERT lifts fraud F1 from 0.83 to 0.86 with LSTM head, 0.74 to 0.76 with MLP - useful for a lesson on whether representation learning beats feature engineering.
Label exclusion in pre-training (isFraud? removed) and fraud upsampling to balance classes as concrete leakage and imbalance handling choices (Sec 2.3).
Origin story of the TabFormer data: 24M transactions, 20,000 users, 12 fields, 29,342 fraud-labelled windows of 2.4M (about 1.2%).

title: FATA-Trans: Field And Time-Aware Transformer for Sequential Tabular Data (Zhang et al., Visa Research/WPI, CIKM 2023, arXiv:2310.13818v1)
topics: Abstract: three disadvantages of replicating static fields (compute overhead, trivialised MLM, ignored time intervals)

1 Introduction: sequential tabular data; Fig 1 static vs dynamic fields in synthetic card transactions; derived static fields (e.g. user average amount); Fig 2 same field values with different order/timing hide anomalies; RNN to transformer history; TabBERT and its two limitations; three listed limitations of prior work; contributions
2.1 Problem definition: windowed sequence X of l records, n_s static + n_d dynamic fields, creation time t_i relative to t_0=0; goal f_theta: X to R (record representations)

2.2 Previous method: TabBERT (field-level transformer then sequence-level transformer; per-field local vocabulary with quantised numerics; static tokens replicated l times; MLM too easy for static fields; no time intervals)
2.3 Proposed method FATA-Trans: two levels (Fig 4)
2.3.1 Static and dynamic field transformers (Eq 4a-4d tokenise+random mask, Eq 5a-5b)

2.3.2 FATA-BERT sequence encoder: field-type embedding, time-aware position embedding (Eq 6a-6b), input = record + position + field type (Eq 7a-7b), outputs (Eq 8), MLM head (Eq 9), loss on masked tokens only (Eq 10)
3.1 Datasets and tasks: synthetic IBM credit-card transactions (anomaly of last txn in window of 10); Amazon Movies&TV and Electronics 5-core (high/low last rating)
3.2 Compared methods: LightGBM, GRU RNN, TabBERT (with time interval added as dynamic field)
3.3 Experimental setup: temporal split, sliding windows, quantisation, 15% masking 80/10/10, pretrain 3 epochs, linear head, 20:1 downsampling, leakage control
3.4 Results (Table 1 AUC; Table 2 pretraining time)
3.5 Ablation study (Table 3)
3.6 Representation visualisation (Fig 5a-f, PCA 3D)
4 Related work: tabular transformers (SAINT, TabNet, TabTransformer, AutoInt), DL vs GBDT studies, sequential recommendation (SASRec, TiSASRec, BERT4Rec, TLSRec, FDSA, BST, SSE-PT, S3-Rec)
5 Conclusion
key_results: Definition (S2.1): a sequential tabular record has n_s static fields (constant within a window, u_i^{s,j}=u^{s,j}) and n_d dynamic fields; static can be raw (card type, issuer) or derived aggregates over a period (average amount, user's average rating).

TabBERT critique (S1, S2.2): replicating static tokens in each of l records costs compute with large n_s or l, and makes MLM trivial because a masked static token is copyable from the other rows' copies.

Architecture (S2.3, Fig 4): Static Field Transformer encodes static fields once (TE_S); Dynamic Field Transformer encodes each row's dynamic fields (TE_D,i); second-level FATA-BERT (BERT-base) takes [IE_S, IE_D,0..IE_D,l-1].
Field-type embedding (S2.3.2): learned lookup with one static and one dynamic vector added to the record embeddings.

Time-aware position embedding (Eq 6): TPos(i)=w_p*i + w_t*t_i + b with trainable scalars w_p, w_t, b, then sinusoidal encoding sin/cos(TPos/10000^(2j/d)); for static input set i=0, t=t_0, so P(0) is shared with dynamic record 0.
Input representation (Eq 7): IE_S = TE_S + P(0) + FE_S; IE_D,i = TE_D,i + P(i) + FE_D.
MLM loss (Eq 10): cross-entropy over masked static and masked dynamic tokens only; masking 15% of each field group, 80% [MASK] / 10% random / 10% unchanged.
Table 1 AUC test: Synthetic txn LightGBM 0.9624, GRU 0.9866, TabBERT 0.9985, FATA-Trans 0.9992; Movies&TV 0.7593/0.7634/0.7964/0.8057; Electronics 0.6962/0.7040/0.7098/0.7206.
Table 2 pretraining time (A100): Synthetic TabBERT 3d11h vs FATA 2d12h; Movies&TV 11h vs 6h33m; Electronics 2d13h vs 1d3h (about 28-55 percent less).

Table 3 ablation AUC (Synthetic / Movies / Electronics): w/o time-aware pos 0.9982/0.8036/0.7108; w/o field-type design (static replicated, no static transformer) 0.9966/0.8038/0.7174; w/o pretraining 0.9970/0.7819/0.7072; full 0.9992/0.8057/0.7206. Pretraining matters most on Amazon data; removing field-type design hurts most on synthetic transactions.
Leakage handling (S3.3): anomaly label excluded from pretraining on the transaction data; on Amazon the rating column of the last review is masked.

Visualisation claim (S3.6): untuned pretrained embeddings separate anomalous vs normal windows, online vs swipe/chip type, and (static-field embeddings) top MCC; TabBERT embeddings fail to separate top MCC.

No proofs; method is motivated by two concrete failure modes of TabBERT and by a toy example (Fig 2), then specified by equations and validated by AUC tables, an ablation and PCA plots. No exercises. Assumes BERT/MLM, transformer position embeddings, AUC, and knowledge of TabBERT (Padhi et al. 2021). Caveats for a course: single run AUC without variance, tiny differences on synthetic data (0.9985 vs 0.9992), sinusoidal formula is only sketched, and Eq 9-10 are garbled in extraction.

Fig 4: side-by-side TabBERT vs FATA-Trans: replicated static tokens into one field transformer per transaction, versus a separate Static Field Transformer (once) and Dynamic Field Transformer (per row), with field-type and time-aware position embeddings summed in the second level. The masked-static-field shortcut (S2.2/S2.3.1): replicate a static field across l rows and MLM can copy it from a neighbour; the fix is to encode static fields once so masked tokens cannot be seen repeatedly.
Static fields can be derived aggregates (average amount, most frequent MCC, user's average rating), so 'static' means constant within the window, not immutable (S1, S3.1).
Time-aware position via a learned linear mix w_p*i + w_t*t_i + b fed into sinusoids; static input pinned at position 0 and t_0 (S2.3.2).
Ablation (Table 3): dropping the static/field-type design costs 0.0026 AUC on synthetic transactions but roughly 0 on Movies, while pretraining is worth about 0.024 AUC on Movies.
Efficiency gem (Table 2): 3d11h to 2d12h pretraining on 24.4M-transaction IBM synthetic data.
Label leakage care (S3.3): drop the label column from pretraining for the fraud data; mask the target rating for the last review.

title: One Transformer for All Time Series: Representing and Training with Time-Dependent Heterogeneous Tabular Data (UniTTab) - Luetto, Garuti, Sangineto, Forni, Cucchiara; arXiv:2302.06375v4, Machine Learning 2025
topics: Abstract: UniTTab, hierarchical Transformer for heterogeneous time-dependent tabular data (e.g. bank transactions), uniform Masked Token pretext task, variable row structure

1 Introduction: GBDTs still dominate tabular; heterogeneity of numeric+categorical; row types (POS vs ATM); four novelties (row-type embedding, sinusoidal numeric embedding, unified masked-token objective with quantized targets, Neighborhood Label Smoothing)
2 Related Work: deep tabular models, Transformers for tabular, LLM/text interfaces for tables (LUNA, GPT-3 prompts), TabBERT as closest work
3 Preliminaries: problem statement (attributes, rows, time series, row types), TabBERT architecture (Field Transformer + Sequence Transformer, Fig. 2a)

4 Method: row-type dependent embedding (Eq.1), frequency-based numeric features (Eq.2), time-stamp split into categorical fields, masked-token training with row and timestamp masking, quantized pseudo-labels, label smoothing and Neighborhood Label Smoothing (Eq.3-5)

5 Experiments setup: five datasets (Pollution, Transaction [synthetic fraud], PKDD'99 Berka, Age2, private RBAT), same architecture, TabBERT protocol, 'our partition' vs 'original partition' for leakage
5.1 Ablation study (Tables 1-3): components, masking strategies, number of frequency pairs L

5.2 Main results: pollution regression (Tab 4-6), fraud detection on synthetic Transaction dataset (Tab 7-8), loan default on Berka (Tab 9), age prediction (Tab 10), churn on RBAT with variable row types (Tab 11)
5.3 Effect of pre-training: pre-training portion vs performance (Tab 12-13)
6 Conclusions and Declarations (code not public, RBAT private)
References
Appendix A: experimental setting, dataset/task definitions, train/test splitting protocols
Appendix B: dataset statistics (Tab B1, B2)
Appendix C: implementation details, regression-loss weighting heuristic lambda (C1-C4), hyperparameters (Tab C3)
key_results: Row-type dependent embedding (Sec 4, Eq.1): g' = W_h g with a per-row-type matrix W_h in R^{m x (d*k_h)}; matrices act as a lookup table for the second Transformer's inputs; inverse S_h for output. Handles rows with different field sets without padding with [MISSING] (Sec 3, 4, 5.2).

Frequency-based numeric embedding (Sec 4, Eq.2): gamma(v)=(sin(2^0 pi v),cos(2^0 pi v),...,sin(2^{L-1} pi v),cos(...)), L=8, then a learnable linear layer; motivated by spectral bias (NeRF analogy). Numeric values are log-scaled and standardized first (App C).
Time stamp split into year/month/day(/hour) categorical fields, each its own field (not summed); treated as categorical works slightly better than numeric (Sec 4).

Unified Masked Token pretext task (Sec 4, Eq.5): mask field with p_f=0.15; row masking p_r=0.1; timestamp fields masked jointly; numeric targets are quantized bins used as pseudo-labels for cross-entropy, never as input; removes need for MSE/CE weighting lambda (App C: lambda=50 Pollution, 25 Transaction by heuristic L_C=lambda L_R).
Neighborhood Label Smoothing (Eq.4): smooth only over bins b-5..b+5 for numeric targets (ordered vocabulary), vs standard LS (Eq.3) for categoricals; eps=0.1.

Ablation (Tab 1): baseline TabBERT 34.30 RMSE / 0.829 F1 -> full 29.05 / 0.850; largest single gain from frequency-based inputs + CE on quantized pseudo-labels (row 4 vs baseline). Tab 2: row masking 0.1 + timestamp masking -> 27.99 / 0.858. Tab 3: L=8 best; F1 collapses to 0.808/0.804 at L=10/12 (sensitive, non-monotonic).

Fraud detection on synthetic Transaction dataset (Tab 7, t=10, F1): fine-tuned UniTTab 0.915, TabBERT repro 0.910, UniTTab+LSTM 0.914, XGBoost 0.779, CatBoost 0.499, VAR 0.495. Tab 8 (t=50): fine-tuning UniTTab 0.812 vs TabBERT 0.777; LSTM UniTTab 0.931; XGBoost 0.349, CatBoost 0.337.

Pollution RMSE (Tab 4 original partition): UniTTab fine-tune 20.05, TabBERT repro 24.10, XGBoost 34.14, CatBoost 34.15, VAR 83.83. Tab 5 (own partition, 5 seeds): UniTTab 25.37+-1.59, XGBoost 48.89, CatBoost 47.09. Tab 6 (t=50): UniTTab 25.11, XGBoost 56.37.

Loan default on Berka (Tab 9, F1, 5 seeds, tmax 50/100/150): UniTTab 0.619/0.654/0.673 (+-0.011-0.038); XGBoost 0.608+-0.079; CatBoost 0.527; VAR 0.474; Random Forest from blog 0.2667 (not comparable, uses other features). Overlapping std devs on the small dataset.
Age2 (Tab 10, F1): UniTTab fine-tune 0.678, TabBERT 0.662, CatBoost 0.622, XGBoost 0.542, VAR 0.354.
Churn on private RBAT (Tab 11, F1): UniTTab 0.604, TabBERT+VRT 0.536, TabBERT 0.526, XGBoost 0.485, CatBoost 0.483, VAR 0.472. VRT alone helps beyond compute savings.

Pre-training effect (Tab 12-13): without pre-training on tiny Berka (478 labeled samples) XGBoost 0.608 beats UniTTab 0.548 and TabBERT 0.526; with full pre-training UniTTab 0.673. Pollution RMSE: 27.10 (no pretrain) -> 23.29 (full).
Direct fine-tuning with [CLS] token beats separate LSTM head on pollution; reverse at t=50 fraud (LSTM 0.931 > fine-tune 0.812) and on Tab 8 TabBERT too (0.883 vs 0.777).

Evaluation caveats stated by authors (App A): TabBERT protocol includes downstream test samples in unsupervised pre-training data; Pollution original stride 5 leaks between overlapping train/test windows, fixed with stride 10; Berka/Age2/RBAT split by client entirely; Berka sequences cut before loan start and loan-payment transactions removed.

Baseline protocol for boosters (Sec 5.2): tsfresh-extracted features (field statistics, autocorrelation lags, local extrema counts), filter feature selection on validation split, grid search for hyperparameters, retrain on train+val; VAR given raw rows with categoricals encoded as integers.
pedagogy: Short research paper (29 pages incl. appendices); method explained with five equations, no proofs. Evidence is ablation tables and benchmark tables, no code released, private dataset for the real-bank claims. Assumes knowledge of Transformers, BERT masked LM, BEiT, label smoothing, XGBoost/CatBoost, LSTM, F1/RMSE. No exercises. Critical-reading notes useful for a course: (1) boosters are fed engineered tsfresh aggregate features, not a tuned sequence/lag feature set, and their F1 swings wildly (CatBoost 0.499 vs XGBoost 0.779 on same data; XGBoost drops 0.779 -> 0.349 when t goes 10 -> 50 while the transformer gets 0.931), which suggests the baseline is not strongly engineered rather than an intrinsic ceiling; (2) the fraud dataset is synthetic with heuristic-rule generation, fraud is highly unbalanced and positives upsampled, and only F1 at a threshold is reported (no PR-AUC, no precision/recall at fixed alert rate, no cost metric); (3) pre-training data includes the downstream test series (unsupervised) on Pollution/Transaction; (4) real-bank gains (churn 0.604 vs 0.485) are on a private unreleased dataset and no standard deviations/seeds are given for Tab 7, 8, 10, 11; (5) no hyperparameter-tuning parity for neural models is described; (6) on the small Berka set XGBoost with no pretraining beats all NN, std devs (0.079 XGBoost) overlap UniTTab; the cited Random Forest 0.2667 is from a blog post and is not comparable; (7) the huge training cost (137M-300M parameters, 4 GPUs, up to 4 days) vs boosting; (8) the same ablation Tab 3 shows F1 swinging 0.858 to 0.808 from L=8 to L=10, hinting at instability. Note UniTTab's own fine-tuned gain over the TabBERT reproduction on Transaction fraud t=10 is only 0.915 vs 0.910.

Scale of full MBD (Sec 3.1-3.2): 2,186,230 clients sampled (1M customers noted in a sentence cut off in extraction); 947,899,612 transactions, 1,117,213,760 geo events, 5,080,781 dialogues; abstract rounds to 950M / 1B / 5M. Table 1 lists MBD as ~2M clients, ~2B events, 'highly imbalanced'.

MBD-small (paper term; HF 'MBD-mini' is a different artefact, see next): all clients with >=1 positive target in the last month plus all-zero clients sampled at 1:10; 69,474 clients, ~80M events (Table 1: 70K clients, 80M events). Used for LLM experiments (Table 6).

MBD-mini (HF card only, not in paper): 'based on 10% of unique clients listed in MBD', same structure and features, shorter span; 5 folds via client_split table (equal numbers of unique clients). Files: client_split.tar.gz 4.2MB, targets.tar.gz 7.9MB, detail.tar.gz 1.97GB (row-per-event parquet-style tables), ptls.tar.gz 1.40GB (pytorch-lifestream format, arrays per client).

Task (Sec 3.2, 4.1): multi-label campaigning, predict purchase of each of 4 products in the month following the reporting date using only events strictly before that month. Purchases labelled monthly Feb 2022 - Jan 2023 (events from 2021-2022). Label balance: 81% of clients no purchase, 15% one, 4% two or more.

Schema (Table 7 + HF card). trx: client_id, event_time, amount, fold, event_type (56 cats), event_subtype (62), currency (15), src_type11 (101), src_type12 (536), dst_type11 (123), dst_type12 (649), src_type21 (40131), src_type22 (87), src_type31 (2389), src_type32 (88). geo: client_id, event_time, geohash_4 (43,999 distinct), geohash_5 (347,698), geohash_6 (2,264,404), fold. dialog: client_id, event_time, 768-d embedding (ruBert-base), fold. targets: mon, target_1..target_4, trans_count, diff_trans_date, client_id, fold. Average 638 transactions per client; only 46% of clients have dialogues, 98% of those <=10.

Anonymization noise (Sec 3.3): IDs hashed with random salt; categoricals mapped to enumerated indices; random noise added to numeric fields AND dates, preserving only the hour of the original date, 'which may cause the local sequence's shuffle'; noise parameters undisclosed; dialogue embedding space divided into regions that are shuffled. Consequence for course: event order within a short window is not trustworthy, timestamps are fuzzed (do not build features that rely on exact inter-event gaps or strict within-day ordering; a leakage/ordering check is a natural lab step).

Anonymization validity (Fig 2, Sec 5.2.1): model ranking on private (original) vs public (anonymized) data has Kendall tau 0.94; absolute AUC lower by ~0.003-0.010 on public data in some cases (e.g. Table 3 Trx Supervised RNN 0.819 public vs 0.813 private; TabGPT 0.802 vs 0.796).

Evaluation: 5-fold out-of-fold; metric = mean ROC AUC over 4 target columns and over 12 monthly reporting dates (Sec 4.1); AUC justified as proxy for A/B-tested campaign revenue (ranking by ROC ~ comparing non-response ratios at all cutoffs). Matching: Recall@1/50/100 with CLIP-style GRU encoders and InfoNCE.

Exact unimodal baselines (Table 2, mean ROC-AUC, MBD): Transactions - Aggregation 0.783+-0.002, CoLES 0.773+-0.002, TabBERT 0.762+-0.004, TabGPT 0.802+-0.002, Supervised RNN 0.819+-0.002. Geostream - Aggregation 0.595, CoLES 0.598, TabBERT 0.603, TabGPT 0.621, Supervised RNN 0.540. Datafusion Trx/Click and Alphabattle also in Table 2 (Alphabattle: Agg 0.785, CoLES 0.793, TabBERT 0.778, TabGPT 0.775, RNN 0.792).

Late fusion on MBD (Table 3): Supervised RNN Trx 0.819, +Geo 0.819, +Dialog 0.821, +Dialog+Geo 0.824; TabGPT 0.802 / 0.800 / 0.810 / 0.808; CoLES 0.773 / 0.775 / 0.781 / 0.783; TabBERT 0.762 / 0.764 / 0.773 / 0.775. Dialogue adds ~1-1.5 pts; geo adds little. Appendix B.3 text: TrxTabGPT + DialogLast ~+1.8% (blending mean) / +3.4% (fusion).

Aggregation baseline detail (Appendix tables 11/13 per-target): public TrxAggregation late-fusion 0.783, TrxTabGPT 0.802, TrxCoLES 0.773, TrxTabBERT 0.762; best public late-fusion DialogLast/Mean + TrxTabGPT 0.810; best private 0.805. Unimodal Dialog alone ~0.586-0.595 public, Geo alone 0.555 (Aggregation) to 0.621 (TabGPT).
Per-target spread (public, TrxTabGPT late fusion): target_1 0.751, target_2 0.844, target_3 0.787, target_4 0.825; target_2 consistently easiest.

Fusion comparison (Table 5): blending is weak (Trx+Dialog 0.742 vs late 0.810-0.821); late fusion with Supervised RNN best on MBD (0.819 Trx+Geo, 0.821 Trx+Dialog); early fusion CrossTransformer 0.815 / 0.821, slightly behind or tied. On Datafusion late TabGPT wins (0.766) and Supervised RNN is worst (0.703).
Matching (Table 4/8): Trx2Geo R@1 0.006, R@50 0.196, R@100 0.303; Geo2Trx 0.004 / 0.162 / 0.262; dialogue pairs essentially zero (R@100 0.001-0.003); Datafusion Trx2Click R@100 0.120.

LLM baselines on MBD-small (Table 6, ROC AUC Trx / Trx+Geo / Geo): Gigar4 0.773 / 0.737 / 0.548; Gigar4 SFT 0.778 / 0.735 / 0.549; Llama3.2-3B 0.773 / 0.735 / 0.534; Qwen2.5-3B 0.757 / 0.727 / 0.539; versus CoLES 0.785 / 0.782 / 0.568; TabGPT 0.779 / 0.782 / 0.594; TabBERT 0.781 / 0.789 / 0.601; Aggregation 0.781 / 0.783 / 0.530; Supervised RNN 0.745 / 0.742 / 0.532. Note Supervised RNN is the weakest on the small set (reverses the full-data ranking) -> data-size effect. LLM inference over MBD-small takes ~12 h on one A100; text serialization 'X-separated' (tab-separated rows), 256 trx or 128 trx + 64 geo, embeddings from last token, PCA to 256, LightAutoML downstream.

Imbalance handling (Table 9): Supervised RNN baseline 0.819, stratified batching 0.819; CoLES 0.773 baseline, undersampling 0.772, oversampling 0.774, class-balanced GBM 0.774 -> rebalancing barely moves AUC.

Hyperparameters (Sec 5.1): pytorch-lifestream defaults; Adam lr 0.001 with StepLR; 15 epochs; 24-d categorical embeddings; CoLES GRU hidden 256; TabBERT/TabGPT 256-d embeddings pooled (min,max,mean,std) to 1024; Supervised RNN GRU hidden 32 with BCE multilabel loss; downstream gradient boosting from PySpark ML; 600-CPU cluster, V100 GPU.

key_results: SETTLED engineered-features figure: 0.816 is the CatBoost official-mean ROC-AUC on test fold 0 only (Tables 7, 8, 9 row fold 0); 0.808 is the mean over five test folds (Table 9 last row; abstract). EventGPT: 0.787 on fold 0 aligned / 0.787 five-fold mean hidden state (abstract says 0.787 vs 0.808 over five folds). Same quantity, different aggregation; the paper states fold 0 scores 0.008 above its five-fold mean (Sec 9).
Weights licence: CC BY 4.0 (HF card tag license:cc-by-4.0; GitHub README: code Apache-2.0, weights CC BY 4.0, the licence of MBD-mini). Not gated.

Size: 22.9M params (paper Sec 6.5; 4.9M tied embedding), HF card says ~23M; width 384, 12 heads x32, 2 event-encoder + 6 history + 2 token-decoder layers; vocab 12,828 tokens. Files per variant: model.safetensors 91,747,056 B (aligned) or 94,106,528 B (aligned-profile, +0.6M params early fusion), vocab.json 235,984 B, config.json ~0.5 KB. So ~92-94 MB per variant. Variants: aligned-s42/s43, aligned-profile-s42/s43, trx-s42/s43, trx-oot-s42/s43 (HF API listing). All hold out test fold 0 only.

Can a notebook run them: yes in principle, small fp32 model; pip install git+https://github.com/deburky/EventGPT; from eventgpt.hub import from_pretrained; model, vocab = from_pretrained('deburky/EventGPT','aligned-s42'); api.embed(model,vocab,cuts,trx,geo) -> (n,384); api.next_event_probs(...) -> (n,5). Neither card nor README states CPU or Colab support; README says only the paper probe embedded 242,604 client-months in ~20 min on one L4 (histories up to 2,048 tokens). Inputs are MBD-mini parquet (hf download ai-lab/MBD-mini, detail.tar.gz). A small demo on a few clients is plausibly CPU-feasible but UNVERIFIED by the source.

Core idea: hierarchical causal transformer; event encoder (bidirectional within event, mean-pool) -> 6-layer causal history decoder over event vectors with temporal RoPE p_i = 64 ln(1 + dt_i/60) -> token decoder conditioned on h_{i-1}; last hidden state at the as-of date (after a 'now' event carrying silence gap) is the customer embedding (Sec 3, Eq 1).

Zero-shot next-event scoring: score = P(name=trx_X) x P(sub=Y | ...) after appending '[EVT] name=trx_X dt=g' to the history; clients who already had the kind get score 0. Five first-occurrence targets ROC-AUC 0.79-0.92 with no labels (Table 4); without the earlier-occurrence rule 50/19 falls 0.91 -> 0.72 (Sec 7.1).

CatBoost on 114 engineered features needs 10,000-300,000 labeled client-months (about 50-400 labeled positives) to match zero-shot; stays below on 23/49 even at 300,000 rows (Figure 10, Tables 6 and 10).

Strong label-free baseline: Markov chain over event kinds (mean over last ten events) x transactions in last 30 days scores 0.79-0.88; EventGPT beats it on 48 of 74 kinds with >=50 positives, lower on 7, median gap 0.042 (Table 3, Sec 7.1).
Frozen embedding + logistic head: official mean 0.787 vs engineered 0.816 (fold 0); token counts over full history 0.803; flat decoder (last token) 0.714, recency-pooled 0.777 (Table 7).

Rank-averaged ensemble of EventGPT(+profile+token counts) with engineered features: 0.830 on fold 0, +0.014 (CI 0.010-0.019); five-fold mean 0.824 vs 0.808, +0.014 to +0.018 on every fold/seed; same ensemble without EventGPT adds only 0.001-0.008, so 0.007-0.016 is EventGPT's own (Tables 8-9, Sec 7.4). Embedding as CatBoost features does not help (0.815 -> 0.808, App C).
Late fusion of 4 profile fields adds 0.013-0.019; target_4 rises 0.754 -> 0.821 (App H).

Leakage/overlap disclosure: pretraining uses 2021-2022 events of the pretraining clients, including the test clients' label months (histories end before label month). Out-of-time run (pretrain on transactions before Feb 2022, 54% of tokens): 0.789 vs 0.793 full-period (matched exposure 0.787) so overlap costs ~0.004-0.006 (Sec 4, Sec 9). Aligned windows leak calendar time via tenure.

Last-month artifact: January 2023 has no transactions so 99.1% rows are churn=1; a model that can date the as-of date scores churn 0.910 vs 0.830 without reading behaviour; they drop January 2023 from churn label (Sec 6.1). Classic label-construction leakage lesson.

Point-in-time guarantee by architecture and data: causal history decoder, history strictly before first day of month, daily geo event stamped at last ping, vocabulary/bins fitted on pretraining folds only (App E). Embeddings from different checkpoints are not comparable (App E).
Hierarchy vs flat decoder: same zero-shot range (0.78-0.92), 2.5x throughput at 2,048 tokens and 4.3x at 4,096, EventGPT loss 1.02 vs 0.94; ~4.75 layer passes/token vs 10 (Sec 7.2, 8, Table 14).

Weights do not transfer across institutions: vocab is the bank's own integer codes (12,828 tokens, 21 amount-bin quantile edges); only dt tokens floor(8 ln(1+ds/8)) are universal; vocab fingerprint stored with checkpoint (Sec 8).
Statistics: DeLong AUC variance clustered by client (Eq 2) because 12 monthly rows per client are correlated; paired SE of model differences is smaller than either model's SE (Sec 6.2).
Delta scoring: rescore only clients with a new event or whose now-token bucket changed; reproduces a full pass exactly; ~90% of MBD-mini clients rescored per day (App B).
Longer windows (4,096/8,192) do not help EventGPT while token counts gain 0.024; block attention within events makes 8,192-token windows affordable (App J).
Seed noise caveat: two seeds differ by up to 0.018 (flat) / 0.022 (EventGPT) across folds; head on a different training draw moves target_2 by up to 0.07 and official mean up to 0.02 (Sec 9).

title: Temporal Contrastive Transformer for Financial Crime Detection: Self-Supervised Sequence Embeddings via Predictive Contrastive Coding (Butvinik, Marcus, Tal, Azoulay; NICE Actimize; arXiv 2605.21490)
topics: Abstract: TCT, CPC-pretrained embeddings fed to XGBoost; embeddings alone AUC 0.8644, raw+emb 0.9205 vs raw 0.9245
1 Introduction: dual fraud/AML mandate; scarce imbalanced labels; heterogeneous transaction data; hypothesis = parity with feature engineering, not gains
2.1 Temporal sequence models for fraud/AML (LSTM, GRU, bidirectional, Transformer; mostly supervised)
2.2 Self-supervised and contrastive learning (BERT, CPC, MoCo, SimCLR, InfoNCE)
2.3 Temporal Fusion Transformer (VSN, GRN, GLU, attention), repurposed from forecasting
2.4 Embedding-based financial crime detection (GNNs, autoencoders, Elliptic)

3 The TCT: 3.1 feature encoding and variable selection; 3.2 hierarchical temporal encoding (short-term LSTM per window, long-term LSTM over window summaries); 3.3 static-dynamic integration (statics dropped because of shortcut learning); 3.4 CPC/InfoNCE objective; 3.5 frozen encoder + XGBoost downstream, LOF/ECOD for unsupervised use
Figures 1-2: architecture and CPC paradigm diagrams

4 Experimental setup: 4.1 data (real retail payments, business entities, chronological split) and preprocessing; 4.2 model config; 4.3 baselines (30 expert features vs concatenation vs embeddings only); 4.4 evaluation (AUC-ROC, ROC curves)
5 Results: 5.1 quantitative (Table 1); 5.2 ROC analysis (curves cross, FPR 0.03-0.06 combined better); 5.3 embedding space (cosine similarity, UMAP by age)

6 Discussion: 6.1 generality fraud/AML; 6.2 why SSL pretraining helps and the key challenge; 6.3 limitations (no relational structure, static shortcut, easy in-batch negatives, shallow XGBoost, attention cost)
7 Conclusion
References (25)
key_results: Null result (Table 1, Sec 5.1): test AUC raw-30-features XGB 0.9245; raw+embeddings 0.9205 (delta -0.004); embeddings-only 0.8644; chance 0.5. Embeddings add nothing over domain features.

Train/val/test AUC: raw+emb 0.992/0.951/0.9205; raw 0.977/0.937/0.9245; emb-only 0.984/0.916/0.8644 -> large generalization gap, worse for embedding configs (Sec 5.1). Val-to-test drop is itself a chronological-split signal.

ROC (Sec 5.2, Fig 3): raw and raw+emb curves nearly identical and cross; combined slightly better at FPR ~0.03-0.06, raw better at higher FPR. At FPR 0.10: TPR ~0.80 (raw and combined) vs ~0.69 (embeddings only). Single split, so delta is not evidence of degradation.

Authors' interpretation (Sec 6.2): embeddings recapture information already in behavioral aggregates (counts, recency, novelty); 'the key challenge is not learning representations but learning ones that capture information not already expressed through engineered features'.

Static-feature shortcut (Sec 3.3, 6.3): injecting static entity attributes into the encoder let the contrastive loss be solved via entity identity rather than temporal dynamics; fix was to use dynamic features only.

Architecture (Sec 3): variable selection network (softmax of GRN over embedded features); hierarchical LSTM encoders (local window length L, then over K window summaries); CPC: z_hat_{t+k} = W_k c_t contrasted with z_{t+k} from encoding the true future window with Enc1; InfoNCE L_k = -E log exp(z_hat^T z/tau)/(exp(.)+sum_j exp(z_hat^T z_j^-/tau)), averaged over K horizons; asymmetry means prediction compared with locally encoded future, not two identical paths.

Training config (Sec 4.2): d = d_h = 32, sequences 15-60 events, 5-6 sub-sequences, AdamW wd 1e-2, one-cycle LR max 1e-3, batch 256 (= number of in-batch negatives), tau = 0.1; XGBoost 100 trees, depth 5, lr 0.3, lambda 1. Pretraining needs >=15 past events + >=3 future; downstream fixed window of 3 events.

Embedding-space observations (Sec 5.3, Fig 4): fraudulent windows show higher variability and lower cosine similarity to surrounding context; UMAP shows smooth age structure though age is not a training signal (qualitative only).

Stated limitations (Sec 6.3): no relational/graph structure, uniform in-batch negatives (no hard-negative mining), deliberately shallow XGBoost, attention cost, no end-to-end fine-tuning; results are single split with one dataset, no confidence intervals, not production-ready.

Framing caveat for a critical reader: abstract spins parity as a win ('approximates domain features without manual engineering'), while body shows no lift; only AUC-ROC reported (no PR-AUC, no precision at fixed review capacity despite heavy imbalance), and frozen embeddings on 3-event windows.

title: FraudTransformer: Time-Aware GPT for Transaction Fraud Detection (Aminian et al., HSBC/Turing/Oxford/Edinburgh; arXiv 2509.23712v2, ICAIF'25 workshop, 9 pp)
topics: Abstract: GPT-style model + time encoder + learned positional encoder vs LR/XGBoost/LightGBM on tens of millions of HSBC events

2 Related Works: GBDT baselines, TabNet/TabTransformer, BERT-style (Fraud-BERT), decoder-only (Stein et al. baseline, social-security GPT), TabFormer hierarchical, FATA-trans

5 Encoding process: binning, ~4000-token vocab, per-column tokenization, token + column embeddings, weight tying

6 Algorithm and Model: GPT 6 layers/8 heads/512 dim/1024 ctx/~20M params (Table 2); time encoding, LayerNorm on time embedding, learned positional embedding, hidden-state update with time gain lambda (Fig 2, Table 1 ablation axes)
7.1 Metrics: PRAUC, AUROC
7.2 Baselines: LightGBM, GPT no-time, XGBoost, Logistic Regression
7.3 Hyperparameter tuning: lambda, f_base, one epoch
7.4 Fraud types: scam, ATO, other; subtype-specific test sets
7.5 Ablation study (Table 3 variants SA, SAP, SR, SRP, RA, RAP, RR, RRP)
7.6 Results (Table 4, Table 5)
7.7 Discussion: PRAUC baseline = prevalence, sinusoidal vs rotary, relative vs absolute, positional encoding, LayerNorm, subtypes

Disclaimer; References [1]-[25]

key_results: Sec 6, Eq (2): hidden update h_bar = h(1) + p_learn + lambda * LN(e_t), h(1)=token emb + column emb; attention blocks unchanged; trained with binary cross-entropy (sequence-level classification, not next-token pretraining).

Sec 3/6: time-id is absolute (t_event) or relative (t_event - t_previous_event); event-level relative chosen over token-level (every token of an event gets the inter-event gap, not 0 within-event). Sinusoidal: e = [sin(theta*id); cos(theta*id)], theta_i = f_base^(-2i/d). Rotary-derived used additively.

Sec 5: every column tokenized separately (identical strings in different columns are distinct tokens), numerics binned, rare/low-risk categories grouped, vocab ~4000, weight tying with LM head; column embedding added to token embedding.

Key reading of Table 4: PE alone lifts transformer from .920 to .947 PRAUC (about +0.027, as large as most of the time-encoder gain); relative time adds ~+0.011 on top; absolute time without PE HURTS (negative deltas). Total SRP margin over LightGBM is only +0.013 PRAUC, +0.006 AUROC.

Table 5 (SRP vs vanilla by subtype): Scam PRAUC .8806->.9337, AUROC .9406->.9704; Other .8477->.8958, .9374->.9627; ATO .8198->.8737, .9329->.9591. Authors argue relative time suits ATO (short temporal windows).
Sec 7.7: PRAUC random baseline equals positive rate, 43% here, so absolute PRAUC looks inflated; authors report deltas vs vanilla GPT instead.
Sec 7.6 + footnote 1: LR/XGBoost/LightGBM std = 0 because deterministic settings (no subsampling); transformer std reported over 3 runs (~0.0001-0.001).
Sec 7.3 + Appendix: best lambda=0.01, f_base=1e7; larger lambda=0.1 and small f_base (1-10) clearly worse; tuned by one-epoch validation PRAUC.
Sec 4: temporal split so test is future data; test fraud rate ~43% obtained by undersampling non-fraud, 'does not represent' real rate; performance on other fraud rates may differ.
Sec 8: FraudTransformer claims 'fewer missed frauds and lower false-alarm rates' with no operating-point (precision at fixed recall/alert rate, cost) evidence given.

Table 4 shows absolute timestamps without a positional encoder make the transformer worse than vanilla (RA -0.0076, SA -0.0050 PRAUC) while relative ones help; with PE absolute is only about neutral (+0.024-0.027, same as NTE). Time-encoder contribution isolated: SRP .9582 vs NTE .9469.
Positional encoder alone (+0.0265 PRAUC) beats LR, XGBoost and almost matches LightGBM (.9454): the 'time-aware' headline is mostly a sequence-order effect.

Zero std dev for baselines (footnote 1): deterministic, no subsampling; compare to 3-seed std ~0.001 for transformers; margin SRP-LightGBM .0128 PRAUC is ~10 std devs of the transformer seeds but ignores baseline variance and data-split variance.

Per-token column embeddings: 'true' in column A differs from 'true' in column B; one-token-per-bin tokenisation of numeric features (vocab ~4000) gives a concrete recipe for turning a transaction row into GPT tokens.
Event-level relative time: all tokens of one transaction share the inter-event gap; contrast with token-level where within-event gaps are 0.
Hyperparameter sensitivity: f_base=1e7, lambda=0.01 best; lambda=0.1 costs ~1-1.5 points PRAUC; f_base=1 costs ~2 points (Tables 6-7).

title: PRAGMA: Revolut Foundation Model (Ostroukhov et al., arXiv:2604.08649v2)
topics: Abstract and Fig 1: one architecture 10M-1B vs task-specific models on six tasks; only relative improvements reported (commercially sensitive), examples synthetic
1 Introduction: text serialisation inflates length and splits numbers into digits; three ways banking histories differ from text; encoder-only rationale; embedding probe vs LoRA; contributions
2.1 Dataset (Fig 2 event timeline): 2.1.1 Event history; 2.1.2 Profile state and life-long events; 2.1.3 Pre-training time range
2.2 Tokenisation (Fig 3, Table 1): key, value (numeric/categorical/text), temporal information
2.3 Model architecture (Fig 4): 2.3.1 token embedding; 2.3.2 profile state encoder; 2.3.3 event encoder; 2.3.4 history encoder; 2.3.5 training (MLM objective, masking strategy, downstream adaptation)
2.4 Training infrastructure: data storage, batching, sequence packing, truncation, pre-training compute
3.1 Evaluation protocol: embedding probing, LoRA, downstream dataset preparation
3.2 Downstream tasks: credit scoring, communication engagement, external fraud, product recommendation, recurrent transactions, LTV
3.3 Main results (Table 2); 3.3.1 scale; 3.3.2 pre-training vs scratch
3.4 Ablations: LoRA vs probe; robustness to event staleness; profile state (Table 3); uplift (Table 4); pre-trained text encoder Nemotron (Fig 5, Table 5); AML limitation (Table 6)
4 Related work: Transformers, masked modelling, tabular Transformers, recommender systems, finance foundation models (nuFormer, TransactionGPT)
5 Conclusion
key_results: Corpus (2.1): 26M user records, 111 countries, 24B events, 207B tokens; 25 months, 2023-2025; no outlier removal or vocabulary pruning.

Training cost (2.4): bf16, Muon + AdamW; S (10M) and M (100M) on 16x H100, L (1B) on 32x H100; S ~2 days, M and L each ~2 weeks wall-clock. LoRA fine-tuning ~1/8 of pretraining time, 12 hours to a few days.

Key-value-time tokenisation (2.2, Fig 3): key = 1 token (~60-key vocab); value vocab ~28k; numerics -> learned percentile buckets plus a zero bucket, one token each; categoricals (manually chosen, e.g. MCC) one token; high-cardinality text -> BPE with [UNK]. Time = soft-log of seconds to last event 8*ln(1+t/8) plus fixed-period cyclical hour/day-of-week/day-of-month features (events only).
Embedding eq.1: x = PosEmb(E(k)) + E(v), one shared table; positions index values within a field, not across fields.

Architecture (Table 1): S 10M d=192, profile/event/history depth 1/5/2, 3 heads; M 100M d=512, 3/16/6, 8 heads; L 1B d=1024, 9/45/18, 16 heads. Three bidirectional encoders: profile state (RoPE on time-since-lifelong-event), event encoder (each event independently, [EVT] token + calendar MLP), history encoder (RoPE on log-seconds to last event). GELU, pre-norm, dropout 0.1.
Life-long events (2.1.2): first-occurrence timestamped key-values (e.g. first_topup) added to profile state so truncation does not lose account-age milestones.

MLM objective (2.3.5): head concatenates event-encoder token output, history output at [EVT], and history output at [USR] (3d, projected to d), logits against embedding table, cross-entropy with label smoothing. Masking: token 15%, whole-event 10%, key-level 10% (all values of a key); some positions replaced by [UNK] excluded from loss as input dropout.

Infra (2.4): LMDB user index + Parquet event shards partitioned by event count; dynamic batching with fixed token budget; varlen attention sequence packing: 2-5x throughput over padded baseline. Truncation: event max 24 tokens (hits 0.01% events), profile 200 tokens, users with >6,500 events keep most recent.

Adaptation (3.1): linear probe on frozen [USR]/last [EVT] embedding (standard-scaled, L-BFGS, minutes to fit; GBDT on 192-d works but slower to tune); LoRA on QKV and MLP, rank 8, alpha 8 (sweep 4/8/16), ~2-4% params.

External fraud, Table 2 vs task-specific baseline (precision/recall): S +0.3/+33.4; M +12.3/+66.4; L +16.7/+64.7 (these are the LoRA-adapted left block). LoRA vs embedding probe at S: +30.8 P / +27.4 R; M +29.8/+24.5; L +23.8/+13.3. LoRA vs scratch PRAGMA-M: +8.0 P / +17.0 R. The paper gives no single 'relative fraud gain' headline number; fraud is reported as precision and recall pairs.
Profile-state ablation (Table 3, PRAGMA-S): external fraud precision +46.8%, recall +85.6% versus event-only model, the largest gain of any task; credit PR-AUC +31.8%.

Credit scoring PR-AUC vs baseline: +70.3 (S), +98.0 (M), +130.2 (L); ROC-AUC +6.2/+10.1/+12.4. Comm. engagement PR-AUC +76.6/+76.7/+79.4. Product rec mAP +10.6/+31.5/+40.5. Recurrent txn F1 +5.2/+5.8/+5.6. LTV near flat (-1.2 to +2.6). Scale gain is task-dependent; S is competitive on LTV/recurrent.

Staleness robustness (3.4.2): dropping recent events within the 99.9th percentile of event-bus propagation delay changes fraud precision/recall by no more than 0.2% relative, credit by no more than 0.9%.
Uplift (3.4.4, Table 4): frozen PRAGMA-L features into a meta-learner: AUUC +163.7%, SNIPS +10.8% over internal baseline.

Text encoder (3.4.5, Table 5): frozen Nemotron-1B-v2 text embedding per field, MSE reconstruction in MLM; PRAGMA-M credit PR-AUC +16.1%, fraud precision +3.8 / recall -0.7, product rec mAP -6.4%; +18% training latency so opt-in only.

AML limitation (3.4.6, Table 6): linear probe on PRAGMA-L embeddings gives F0.5 -47.1% versus the production network-aware baseline. Two reasons given: large AML dataset lets the baseline learn alone, and AML is relational (cross-record network features) while PRAGMA sees each history in isolation.

Evaluation caveats: relative deltas only ((x/baseline - 1)%), internal tasks and baselines, no absolute metrics, no public data, no uncertainty intervals; the fraud task is described only as 'external fraud' binary classification with precision/recall.

key_results: WHAT THE 22.5% IS (Sec 5.1, Table 4, p.13): the row 'TGPT-3D-FMT - FMVTL + LLM' has AD (%) RI = +22.5. AD is 'a proprietary metric ... measures the accuracy under an operational threshold'; its formulation is withheld 'for company policy compliance' and only the relative improvement (RI) over the production model is reported. It is a relative improvement, not an absolute accuracy, not a precision/recall/AUC, not a fraud detection rate; the production baseline's absolute value is never given.

Is it fraud? The paper never uses the word fraud for the task. The label is 'anomaly transaction detection' / 'anomaly prediction' ('Given that anomalies are rare events...'). Dataset T-JGC: 2 classes, ~400 downstream features, 'a key revenue-driven product' (Sec 4.1, Table 3); the product and the label definition are undisclosed. Fraud appears only in the references (Bahnsen 2016 feature engineering for credit card fraud; Liu 2021 fraud GNN; FraudTransformer, Aminian 2025). So 22.5% = relative gain on an undisclosed anomaly metric under an undisclosed operating threshold against an undisclosed production model; calling it a fraud-detection improvement is an inference the paper does not make.

Abstract says 'significantly improves ... anomaly transaction detection performance against a competitive production model'; intro bullet says '22% relative improvement ... on a business-critical anomaly detection metric'.

Caveats on the 22.5% (all from Sec 5.1): the best row is the +LLM-initialised MCC embedding variant; the plain 3D-FMT (FMVTL) is +19.2; FMVTL-2 +15.5; MTF +14.6/+9.5; 2D w/Feat +7.3; instance-level Feat-Transformer (no sequence) is already +7.7, so TGPT-2D with full sequences gives no gain over a single-transaction model; models without features are -87 to -90.5; 1D w/Feat -9.1; FVTL -12.9. Production model is trained on the downstream dataset without missing fields, TGPT on the merged dataset with 'bubbles' (metadata-only rows). Test set is a later time period than train. Single reported number per variant, no confidence intervals or seeds; each model trained separately per dataset ('train and evaluate TGPT on each of them separately').

Table 6 (Sec 5.4): scalability tricks effect on AD relative to the 3D base: compositional embedding -22.6% memory / +1.9% performance; local attention -24.9% / +2.8%; weight tying -73.8% / -0.6%. Authors speculate the AD task 'may not favor long-term transaction dependencies' and compact models curb overfitting.

Transaction as MMTT data (Sec 2.1): tr = [M (+) E (+) F]; M numeric metadata (amount, timestamp), E entities (merchant ID, MCC, location), F optional task features (hundreds to thousands of mostly numeric/categorical values, low cardinality). Metadata 10-20 fields; merchant ID may have millions of values.

3D architecture (Sec 3.1-3.3): metadata Transformer (bidirectional encoder over the fields of one transaction), feature Transformer (over F), temporal Transformer (decoder-only, causal, over transactions). Variants: 1D (MLP over fields + temporal TF), 2D (metadata TF replaces MLP; features concatenated into same fields), 3D-MTF (late fusion: history omits features; the predicted next-transaction embedding is split into segments of size d_f and fed with the feature embeddings to the feature TF), 3D-FMT (early fusion: feature TF -> VTL -> metadata TF -> VTL -> temporal TF).

Virtual Token Layer (Sec 3.3.2, Fig 3, Eq 9-10): linear channel (softmax-normalised parameter matrix, linear combinations of input embeddings, can stack/segment to change token size) plus nonlinear channel (one-layer MLP), summed; described as a scalable ResNet-style block. Produces v_f virtual feature tokens and v_t virtual transaction tokens per transaction, decoupling information bandwidth from embedding size; the temporal TF sees v_t*n tokens.

Time encoding (Table 2): time gap, month, year (since 2000), day of week, day of month. Numerics embedded by MLP(log(m+eps)); categorical by trainable embeddings, one shared dim d_M; one-hot positional encoding of fields slightly beat sinusoidal.

Compositional (hashed) embedding (Sec 3.2.3, App A): k hash functions (MurmurHash3) map n ids to m<<n slots, mean-pooled with EmbeddingBag; index 0 for unseen entities. Motivating number: 10M merchants x 128 dim = 1.3B parameters.
Weight tying (Sec 3.5): merchant logits = E_e(E_tr)^T, no separate huge classification head.

Losses (Eq 11-15): squared error on log(y+eps) for numeric targets (time gap, amount in US cents); cross-entropy for merchant and MCC; optional supervised loss; weight decay; VTL orthogonality losses ||E_lin E_lin^T - I||_F^2. Four self-supervised targets: time gap, amount, merchant, MCC.

Theorem 1 (Sec 3.4, App B): if 1<d_f<<d_M, 1<v_f,v_t,|M|<<|F|, 1<w<<d_tr/v_t then O(3D-FMT) << O(2D); temporal term ratio tends to 1/v_t. Local attention cuts causal attention cost from O(|S|^2 d) to O(w^2 d). FMT inference latency ~2.5x MTF, within SLA.

Generation results (Table 4): no-feature 1D/2D reach ~49% MCC Rec@1 (of ~800) and >30% merchant Rec@1 (of 3M); Transformers4Rec 33.46% MCC; 3D-FMT best on most metrics (MCC 49.94-50.12, merchant up to 32.73, time MAE 0.0686 for +LLM). Features barely help the generative task without proper fusion.

Dining trajectory (Table 5a): next-restaurant Rec@1/Rec@50 of 500K: SASRec 11.9/38.5, TGPT-1D 12.8/42.5, TGPT-2D 14.2/45.6, 2D merchant-head-only 13.7/43.8 (auxiliary heads help). Table 5b location accuracy from predicted restaurants: top-1 28% zip, 42% city, 84% state; top-10 60/69/91%.

TGPT-2D (56M params incl. embeddings) beats the best fine-tuned LLM (Llama2-7B) on next-MCC prediction with 92% fewer parameters and 300x faster inference (0.27 ms vs 84.9 ms) (Sec 5.3, Fig 6); LLMs fine-tuned with LoRA/FSDP, MCCs as 800 new special tokens.

Data scaling (Fig 4): AD and generative metrics improve with more training transactions; 3D advantage over 2D appears only at larger data volumes; model capacity not yet scaled (10.3M params excluding embeddings).

Design lessons (Sec 6): BatchNorm beat LayerNorm; Pre-LN inside transformers; d_tr 64->128 helps, 256 OOM on A100-80GB; five Integrate strategies (concat, MLP compression, pooling, field selection + pooling, field selection + concat) with trade-offs in Table 7; encoder-only temporal TF fine for 1 step and better short-horizon but suffers context erosion, decoder-only better long-horizon; focal loss / class weights gave no gain over plain CE; BF16 curbs overfitting on small data, FP32 better when scaling data.

LLM embedding init (App C): MCC embeddings from last-layer activations of an open-weights LLM prompted with the Visa Merchant Data Standards Manual description; gives the 22.5% row vs +19.2 from scratch.

Fusion taxonomy (Sec 3.3, Fig 4): early fusion = pretrained embeddings + tabular into GBT; late fusion = finetune transformer then GBT on embeddings+features; joint fusion = end-to-end; GBTs cannot join because no gradient flows to transformer

Scaling (Sec 4.2): 24M -> +0.37%, 330M -> +0.62% (at 20M rows baseline config); longer context helps, larger model exploits it better; more finetune data helps, bigger models gain more

title: A Foundation Model for Multimodal Event Sequences in Financial Applications (Rusakov et al., Sber, KDD '26, arXiv 2607.09955v1)

key_results: Sec 3: objective is a task-independent frozen embedding Phi_core: {S_u^(1..M)} -> z_u in R^D, used together with engineered features f_u; early fusion = merge all modalities into one chronological event sequence (vs late fusion, modelled independently).

Sec 4.1.2 Event Encoder: variable attribute set per event type, embedded to R^d, padded to N_attr with mask; self-attention over the attribute axis (padded positions masked in softmax); masked mean over attributes + LayerNorm gives one fixed-size event vector -> homogeneous sequence X in R^{T x d}.

Sec 4.1.3-4.1.4: GPT-2-like causal transformer; user embedding z_seq = mean pooling over time of final-layer outputs; loss L_t = sum CE over observed categorical attrs of event t+1 + sum MSE over observed numerical attrs (missing attrs from other modalities ignored).

Sec 4.2 TabNN: signed log x'=sign(x)log(1+|x|) then standardise; numeric embedding = trainable vector times normalised value; categorical embedding tables; noise added to embeddings in training; transformer across features; learnable weighted-sum aggregation z_tab.
Sec 4.3: z_u=[MLPadapter(z_seq), z_tab] -> task head; only TabNN, adapter, head trained; sequence encoder frozen. Baselines: TabNN alone; sequence embedding alone.
Sec 4.4.1: next-event prediction beat CoLES, MLM and DeTPP as pretraining objective (empirical, no numbers given). 4.4.2: TabNN beat FFN, DCNv2, TabM.

Table 2 (42M): ROC AUC Task1-4 avg: engineered features 0.681/0.732/0.891/0.866 avg 0.792; pretrained only 0.704/0.727/0.872/0.846 avg 0.787; pretrained+features 0.705/0.742/0.892/0.864 avg 0.801 (+0.009). Embeddings alone win on Task 1, lose on 3 and 4; combination is consistently better.

Table 3 scaling (avg AUC): 2M 0.750 alone / 0.792 with TabNN; 8M 0.774 / 0.796; 42M 0.787 / 0.801. Gains from scale are much smaller when engineered features present (0.792->0.801 vs 0.750->0.787); beating baseline 0.792 needs enough scale.
Table 4 context length (8M): 256 avg 0.790, 512 0.792, 1024 0.795; longer history helps all tasks.
Table 5 pretrained vs same architecture supervised end-to-end (8M): 0.795 vs 0.791 avg (+0.004); biggest gain Task 1 (0.693 vs 0.684); explained by labelled data being far smaller than unlabelled.
Table 6 modalities (8M): Txn 0.792; Txn+Comm 0.793; Txn+Comm+Click 0.796; Task 2 gains >0.01 (0.729 -> 0.741).

Split (NVIDIA): temporal, by cumulative transaction count ordered by date: first 80% train, next 10% validation, final 10% test; disjoint ordered windows to prevent leakage.

Baseline (NVIDIA): GPU XGBoost, tree_method=hist, device=cuda, trained on a 1M-row balanced training sample; evaluated on a 100k stratified holdout keeping ~0.1% fraud. Raw features: 13 hand-engineered tabular features (the individual features are NOT listed in the post). Test ROC-AUC 0.9885, test AP 0.1238.
Metric argument: under ~0.1% imbalance ROC-AUC saturates and hides differences; AP (area under precision-recall) is the primary metric.

Model: compact Llama decoder, ~29M params, hidden 512, 8 layers, GQA with 8 query and 2 KV heads, 8,192-token RoPE context, SwiGLU, RMSNorm, vocab 6,251; causal LM (next-token prediction); 30-step demo drops loss from ln(6251)~8.74 (random guess) to ~6.0; repo ships a 3,000-step checkpoint.

Embeddings: final hidden layer, last-non-pad-token pooling (causal attention means only last position has seen the whole history), 512-dim per user history, batch 1024; saved as .npy with metadata.json for row alignment.

Table 1 (TabFormer temporal test split, 100k stratified): Raw 13 features ROC-AUC 0.9885 AP 0.1238; Embeddings only (512d PCA to 64d, ~78% variance) 0.8775 / 0.0123; Combined 77d (13 raw + 64) 0.9925 / 0.1755. Embeddings alone underperform the raw baseline; value comes from combining event-level row features with sequence-level history context.

title: Understanding Structured Financial Data with LLMs: A Case Study on Fraud Detection (FinFRE-RAG) — Tan, Ma, Zhang, arXiv 2512.13040v2
topics: Abstract and 1 Introduction: tabular input misalignment; fraud ambiguity and rarity; contributions
2 Related Work: 2.1 fraud detection; 2.2 LLMs for finance; 2.3 in-context learning and RAG

3 Method: 3.1 problem setup (D_ext, D_test); 3.2 offline feature reduction (RF importance, top-k, z-score normalisation); 3.3 online retrieval-augmented ICL (categorical back-off filter, cosine top-n, prompt construction)
4.1 Setup: datasets, models, metrics (F1, MCC), implementation, LoRA fine-tuning
4.2 Results: RQ1 baseline vs FinFRE-RAG (Table 1); RQ2 k and n sensitivity (Fig 2, 3); RQ3 feature-selection ablation (Table 2); RQ4 risk score vs binary (Table 3); RQ5 fine-tuning vs RAG (Table 4)
4.3 Further analysis: behavioural differences (Fig 4); why Gemma 3 wins on CCF/PaySim; PaySim label-homogeneous neighbourhoods
5 Conclusion; Limitations; Ethical considerations
Appendix A datasets (Table 5); B hyperparameters and baseline tuning (Table 6, 7); C prompts (Table 8); D inference efficiency (Tables 9, 10)
key_results: Method (Sec 3): two stages. Offline: train an untuned Random Forest on D_ext, rank features by importance, keep top-k (k=10), z-score numerics with global mu/sigma (Eq 1). Online: categorical equality filter added progressively by importance with back-off to the largest non-empty candidate set (Eq 2), then cosine similarity over normalised numeric features (Eq 3) to get top-n (n=20) labelled neighbours, serialised as natural-language sentences ending 'It is a fraud / It is not a fraud', plus the query without label.
Output is a 1-5 risk score (>=4 means fraud) plus a short explanation, not a binary answer (Sec 4.1, RQ4).

Table 1 (Sec 4.2 RQ1): bare LLMs are near random (e.g. Qwen3-14B MCC -0.01 on CCF, F1 0.00 on CCF and PaySim). With FinFRE-RAG Qwen3-14B F1 goes 0.00->0.31 CCF, 0.14->0.48 CCFraud, 0.04->0.62 IEEE-CIS, 0.00->0.11 PaySim; MCC to 0.36/0.46/0.60/0.22.

Table 1 best LLM: Gemma 3-27B + RAG F1 0.79 CCF (MCC 0.78), 0.73 PaySim; Gemma 3-12B + RAG CCFraud F1 0.59. Tabular baselines (F1/MCC): XGBoost CCF 0.89/0.89, IEEE-CIS 0.74/0.73 (F1 0.74 is fraud-ML baseline; LLM best IEEE-CIS 0.66/0.64), TabM best on CCFraud 0.66/0.65, IEEE-CIS 0.82/0.82, PaySim 1.00 F1. LLMs still lag specialised classifiers on IEEE-CIS and CCF mostly; competitive or above RF/XGB on CCFraud (RF 0.52, XGB 0.48 vs Gemma 12B 0.59) and PaySim (XGB 0.55 vs Gemma 0.71-0.73).

RQ2: more features does not help; best MCC with a compact top-k (sweep 5-25 on CCF and IEEE-CIS, Fig 2). Reasoning models (Qwen3-14B, GPT-OSS-20B) keep improving with larger n (IEEE-CIS Qwen MCC 0.3->0.45, GPT-OSS 0.34->0.43); non-reasoning Gemma 3 shows diminishing/negative returns beyond some n because it leans on the fraction of fraud labels among neighbours (Fig 3).
RQ3 (Table 2): importance-ranked features beat random-k features; IEEE-CIS Qwen3 F1 0.62 vs 0.27, MCC 0.60 vs 0.32; CCF Qwen 0.31 vs 0.26.
RQ4 (Table 3): 5-level score beats binary output on most dataset/model cells (e.g. IEEE-CIS Qwen F1 0.62 vs 0.51; PaySim Gemma 0.71 vs 0.26); exception CCF Qwen where binary is higher (0.49 vs 0.31).

RQ5 (Table 4): LoRA fine-tuned (binary output, no explanation) LLMs do not consistently beat RAG; FT has higher precision, lower recall (IEEE-CIS Qwen FT P 0.71, R 0.41 vs RAG P 0.61, R 0.63); FT wins on CCFraud for Qwen/GPT-OSS but loses on IEEE-CIS for all three.

Sec 4.3: with RAG the rationale compares query with retrieved cases and weighs feature deltas; without it the model uses surface priors (gmail domain) (Fig 4). Failure mode: PaySim test has 13 positives; for 11 neighbours were all positive, for 2 all negative, so recall is a uniform 0.85 across models; predictions are skewed by label-homogeneous retrieval rather than feature evidence. Gemma 3 uses a majority-vote shortcut.

Appendix D (Tables 9, 10): RAG raises mean input tokens from ~160-260 to ~1500-2960; generation latency (vLLM, batch 1, retrieval excluded) is not systematically worse: Qwen3-Next-80B IEEE-CIS 45,497 ms -> 19,905 ms (output tokens 5369 -> 2336), Qwen3-14B CCF 18,237 -> 13,838 ms; but GPT-OSS-20B CCFraud 1,638 -> 2,638 ms and Qwen3-14B PaySim 9,774 -> 12,904 ms. Non-reasoning Gemma 3 about 1.0-1.6 s; reasoning Qwen3 ~8-45 s per query.

Limitations (Sec Limitations): main text reports no latency/throughput/serving cost (added only in App D, generation time only); datasets are mostly toy-like, IEEE-CIS and CCF have anonymised feature names; no human evaluation; cosine retrieval only; explanations are heuristic, not causal. PaySim balance columns leak labels (App A).

key_results: Table 2 (Sec 4.3.1), test set 5,000 orders with 9.6% fraud: zero-shot frontier models have F1 only 0.12-0.18 (GPT-4.1 0.1491, GPT-5-mini 0.1461, Claude Sonnet 4.5 0.1503, Gemini 2.5-Flash 0.1615, Qwen3-235B 0.1806, DeepSeek-V3 0.1487, Kimi-K2 0.1265, GLM-4.5 0.1219). Precision about 0.09-0.11, i.e. near the 9.6% base rate, so close to chance ranking.

Frontier precision ~0.10 with widely varying recall/specificity: models differ mostly in where their implicit threshold sits (Qwen3-8B non-thinking: TPR 0.84, TNR 0.21; GPT-5-mini TPR 0.225, TNR 0.80), not in discrimination.

GSPO standard setup (GSPO.S): Qwen3-4B F1 0.3594 (prec 0.308, TPR 0.431, TNR 0.894), 8B F1 0.3598 (acc 0.8545), 14B F1 0.3467; F1 gains of +120.90%, +98.35%, +105.27% over base; specificity +336% for 8B. Beats all frontier baselines about 2x.
Calibration gap thesis: general LLMs spot the signals (proxy IP, long shipping distance) but lack a task-specific decision threshold; RL on labels calibrates the latent boundary.
Emergent brevity: GSPO shrank average completions 62.92% (4B), 28.60% (8B), 29.13% (14B) without length penalty (e.g. 4B 761.8 -> 282.5 tokens).
Compressed setup (predefined signals + enforced brevity, 60-96 tokens) gives only +10.57%, +5.73%, +9.35% F1 (F1 0.18-0.19): exploration and room to reason matter.

Inverse scaling of faithfulness: 4B and 8B keep >80% DeepEval hallucination pass rate; 14B drops 46.7 points, interpreted as reward hacking (fabricated persuasive evidence). Stricter judge criterion: any factual error fails.
Eq.3-4 GSPO: sequence-level importance ratio s_i = exp(mean token log-ratio), clipped, advantage A_i = (r_i - mean)/std within the group of G rollouts; no per-token 1/|y| outside the objective.
Reward: accuracy reward weighted 2.5x format reward; outcome reward only, process rewards avoided for reward-hacking risk.

Data protocol (Sec 4.1, Table 1): train 4,900 (about balanced, Jun-Dec 2023), test 5,000 at 90.4%/9.6% (Jan-Jun 2024), chronological split; balanced training needed else accuracy reward is gamed by predicting all legit.
