title: Explainable AML Triage with LLMs: Evidence Retrieval and Counterfactual Checks (Torres, Cheng, Hu; arXiv 2604.19755)
topics: Abstract: evidence-constrained LLM triage; headline PR-AUC 0.75, Escalate F1 0.62
1 Introduction: alert volume and false positives, RBA and audit expectations, graph ML for AML, synthetic data (SynthAML10, AMLSim), LLM hallucination risk, three contributions

2 Problem setup: 2.1 triage as decision-and-evidence task; 2.2 inputs (alert metadata m, transactions T, customer K, policy corpus P, case memory H); 2.3 output space (disposition, confidence, rationale, evidence set, next actions); 2.4 counterfactual checks; 2.5 requirements R1-R8

3 Method: 3.1 overview; 3.2 evidence representation and hybrid retrieval; 3.3 LLM triage under provenance constraints plus verifier/repair loop; 3.4 counterfactual checks (decision and evidence counterfactuals); 3.5 end-to-end procedure

4 Datasets and setup: 4.1 SynthAML10, AMLSim, Elliptic; 4.2 label mapping to dismiss/monitor/escalate; 4.3 evidence corpus construction; 4.4 time-aware 70/10/20 split and retrieval leakage control; 4.5 six baselines; 4.6 model and retrieval configuration
5 Evaluation protocol: 5.1 triage effectiveness; 5.2 evidence quality and auditability; 5.3 counterfactual robustness and faithfulness; 5.4 safety and failure modes
6 Results: 6.1 effectiveness under imbalance (Table 1); 6.2 auditability; 6.3 counterfactual faithfulness; 6.4 numerical and policy hallucination
7 Discussion: operations, auditability and model-risk governance, generalization limits, security/privacy/misuse, cost and latency, limitations
8 Conclusion and references (28)
key_results: Framing (Abstract, 1, 2.1): AML triage is a decision-and-evidence task, not only classification; the LLM is a component in a governed system, not a free-form text generator.

Output contract (2.3, 3.3, 4.6): disposition in {dismiss, monitor, escalate}, calibrated confidence, optional ranked typologies, rationale with citations, supporting vs contradicting/missing evidence IDs, explicit unknowns, next actions. Every paragraph of the rationale needs at least one evidence reference.

Evidence item (3.2): stable ID, source type, effective timestamp, access-control label. Hybrid retrieval = structured filters (customer ID, time window, rule type, geography, product, ACL) then semantic ranking, with per-type quotas, dedup, diversity, latest-effective-policy preference and hard ACL filtering before the model sees anything.

Verifier-and-repair loop (3.3): provenance integrity (all cited IDs exist in the bundle) and numerical/temporal consistency (amounts, dates, ordering, thresholds); on failure, targeted feedback and regeneration.

Two counterfactual families (3.4): decision counterfactuals (minimal plausible edit delta so that f(a + delta) != f(a): toggle indicator, change counterparty risk tier, narrow/widen window, remove one graph path) and evidence counterfactuals (remove or substitute a key evidence item e* and check the rationale stops citing it and reacts in the expected direction). Test against 'decorative citations'.

Counterfactual acceptance (3.4): a candidate is accepted only with flip validity (validator risk score or disposition changes; validator is a rules engine and/or light scoring model) and rationale alignment (re-run citations and drivers match the modified facts). Edits are bounded by an edit budget and plausibility rules.

Metrics (5.2-5.4): citation validity, evidence support rate, coverage of decision drivers (needs one policy/typology item plus one case/customer/transaction item), citations per alert; CF-Flip Rate, Evidence-Faithfulness under Removal, CF-Stability under irrelevant perturbations; numerical inconsistency rate, policy hallucination rate, unsupported assertion rate, adversarial conflicting-evidence test.

Table 1 (6.1): Rule/threshold PR-AUC 0.41, P 0.18, R 0.78, F1 0.29. GBDT 0.63, P 0.42, R 0.66, F1 0.51. GNN 0.69, P 0.46, R 0.71, F1 0.56. LLM-only 0.52, P 0.31, R 0.60, F1 0.41, citation validity 0.62, evidence support 0.54, CF-flip 0.28, faithfulness 0.39, numerical inconsistency 0.11, policy hallucination 0.14. RAG 0.71, P 0.49, R 0.73, F1 0.59, 0.96, 0.83, 0.41, 0.57, 0.06, 0.05. Full system 0.75, P 0.53, R 0.75, F1 0.62, 0.98, 0.88, 0.58, 0.76, 0.03, 0.02.
Central finding (6.1): LLM alone is below the classical ML baselines; the gain over GNN comes from precision at similar recall (0.53 vs 0.46 at recall 0.75 vs 0.71).

Leakage controls (4.4): time-ordered 70/10/20 split by alert time; case memory indexes training cases only; no test labels or post-decision artifacts in retrievable text, because retrieval can become a label channel.
Cost control (7.5): lightweight scoring first, then route only the top x% or ambiguous alerts through the full pipeline; cap counterfactuals at 1-2 per alert and cap repair iterations.

Governance (7.2, 7.4): counterfactuals are decision support, not ground truth; the audit trail is logs of retrieved evidence, outputs, verifier failures and counterfactual outcomes; risks include prompt injection via untrusted documents and counterfactuals acting as evasion instructions.

pedagogy: A systems and applied-methods paper, not a textbook: no proofs, no code, no released artefacts or exercises. The method is described in prose with three block diagrams (Figures 1-3) and one PR curve (Figure 4). Prerequisites: basic RAG, AML alert and triage vocabulary, precision/recall/PR-AUC. Caveats for a course designer: all results are on synthetic data (SynthAML10, AMLSim); the paper reports no seeds, confidence intervals or specific LLM names; Section 5.3 refers to a 'Section 4.7' that does not exist; the Table 1 text extraction is garbled, though the numbers above were checked against the 6.x prose. Treat the numbers as illustrative, not as established benchmarks. Introduction citations [7]-[12], [14]-[16], [22]-[26] are largely tangential padding.
figures: Figure 1 (3.1): end-to-end architecture. Alert -> evidence retrieval -> LLM with provenance constraints -> verifier -> counterfactual module -> triage record. Worth recreating as a pipeline diagram.
Figure 2 (3.3): evidence bundle construction, labeled blocks (policy, KYC, triggers, transactions, similar cases) with stable IDs and the provenance constraints.
Figure 3 (3.4): counterfactual check workflow. Extract claimed drivers, propose bounded edits, validate flip, re-run the LLM, check rationale alignment.
Figure 4 (5.1): precision-recall curves for all methods. Redraw from Table 1 numbers if wanted; it is illustrative only.

Idea for a new figure: ablation bar chart of Table 1 (LLM-only -> RAG -> RAG+CF) across PR-AUC, citation validity and hallucination rates, showing that grounding gives most of the gain and counterfactuals add the rest on faithfulness.
Idea for a new figure: a structured triage record with highlighted citations, plus the same record re-run after removing evidence e* (the 'decorative citation' test).
gems: Decorative citations (3.4): a model can cite relevant-looking passages while its decision does not depend on them. The test is to remove the cited item and see whether the answer and citations change. A concrete, teachable faithfulness test.
LLM-only is below GBDT and GNN (PR-AUC 0.52, F1 0.41, against 0.63/0.51 and 0.69/0.56) but RAG lifts it to 0.71/0.59 (6.1). The value is the system, not the model.

Provenance table (6.2): LLM-only citation validity is 0.62 and evidence support 0.54, so roughly 4 in 10 citations are fabricated. With retrieval and a verifier it is 0.96 to 0.98. 'A single fabricated policy reference can invalidate the entire record.'
Rules baseline: recall 0.78 but precision 0.18 (F1 0.29), the standard false-positive burden of threshold monitoring (6.1).
Retrieval as a label channel (4.4): indexing test cases or post-decision notes into case memory leaks labels. Train-only case memory, time-ordered split.
Verifier feedback strings (3.3): 'you referenced an evidence ID that is not present' and 'your total amount conflicts with evidence e_T3'.
Absence of evidence is evidence (3.3): the contract forces the model to separate supporting from contradicting or missing evidence and to fill an 'unknowns' field.
Explainability metric 'coverage of decision drivers' (5.2): a justification needs both what rule/typology it matches and what in the customer/transaction context supports it.
Cost routing (7.5): run the full pipeline only on the top x% risk or ambiguous alerts; at most 1-2 counterfactuals and few repair iterations.

key_results: Sec 10 / Table 1 (p.12): six domain-expert investigators from one global fintech rated AI-drafted SARs on 1-5 scales. Narrative completeness 3.52 (70%); Efficiency gains in investigation 3.06 (61%); Financial transaction analysis 3.50 (70%); Volume/velocity 4.00 (80%); Jurisdictional risk 3.80 (76%); Communications/text pattern 4.00 (80%); Location anomaly 5.00 (100%); Account integrity 4.67 (93%); Dispute/chargeback 4.50 (90%). Percent = average score / 5 (3.06/5 = 61.2%), i.e. a normalised rating, not a measured quantity.

TIME-SAVING CHECK (the reason this source is canon): NO time saving was measured. Sec 10 states investigators rated 'efficiency (time saved using the draft)'; scores averaged and 'normalized to percentage values'. The '61% time savings' is the mean 3.06/5 perceived-efficiency rating re-expressed as a percent. No stopwatch, no with/without-tool baseline, no handling-time data, no sample size beyond 6 raters, no number of drafts stated, no inter-rater agreement. Yet Sec 10 bullet says 'Time Savings (61%)' and the Conclusion (Sec 12) says drafts '70% complete on average, saving investigators significant time (around 61%)' -- an over-reading of a subjective rating. The only quantitative time figure that is not a rating is the FinCEN 25-315 minutes estimate for final SAR preparation stages (Sec 1), which is background, not a result.

Efficiency was the lowest-rated component in Table 1 (3.06, barely above the scale midpoint 3); 70% completeness is also a rating, and 'reaches 87% in specific typologies' (Sec 10) with no typology breakdown given.

Sec 3.2: direct prompting of GPT-4 / Claude 3 on raw AML case data worked on clean template cases but degraded on multi-subject, multi-typology, long-history cases; hallucinated interactions and transactions; and 'the required manual validation and correction nullified any time benefits'. Qualitative, no numbers (cites 20-30% hallucination rates from [7]). Note the tension: the paper's own baseline observation is that review cost can erase drafting speed, while its own system's time claim is never measured.

Sec 5 architecture: Data ingestion -> AI-Privacy Guard -> Crime Type Detection (risk-indicator tools + Random Forest/Gradient Boosting typology classifiers giving ranked typologies with confidence) -> Planning Agent spawns typology agents and External Intelligence Agent -> Narrative Generation Agent (CoT) -> Compliance Validation Agent -> Feedback Agent -> investigator, with dynamic memory underneath.

Sec 5.3: privacy masking sits upstream of any external LLM; entities are anonymised before typology agents/LLMs, unmasked into narrative drafts for investigators, re-masked before external feedback systems. Model: RoBERTa + CRF, quantised and DeepSpeed-accelerated for SLA.
Sec 5.6 seven typology agents: transaction fraud, payment volume velocity, country risk, textual content, geographic anomaly, account health, dispute pattern.

Sec 7: pre-production evaluation compares AI narratives with investigator-written SARs against golden datasets: 'Intro scoring' (date ranges, amounts, subject ID; weighted accuracy), 'Narrative scoring' (seven compliance dimensions; semantic similarity with category weights), aggregated weighted final score; Gemini 2.5 Pro as independent judge. No scores reported.

Sec 8: Compliance Validation Agent (Agent-as-a-Judge) cross-checks narrative amounts, dates, jurisdictions, identities against parsed data and typology-agent outputs using rule-based logic plus LLM semantic coherence, and checks regulatory memory (e.g. negative-news references present). Flags go to Feedback Agent -> investigator.

Sec 2.1 regulatory facts: SAR e-filing within 30 days of detection (60 if subject unidentified); six required elements (subject, activity description, institution, filer contact, narrative, supporting documentation kept 5 years); narrative must not 'tip off' the subject.
Sec 9 stance: human-in-the-loop, 'not approve-and-go'; drafts are initial, meant for expert refinement.

Limitations visible in the text: single institution, six raters who also appear to be colleagues of the authors (acknowledgments thank the investigations team), no baseline/control, no ground-truth accuracy metric reported despite the Sec 7 framework, no ablation of agents or memory, no hallucination rate for the system, no cost/latency figures.

key_results: Best config: Gemini 4 Argon at high reasoning, 42% pass; Opus 5.5 36% at $1.54 vs Argon $1.65 per rollout; GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol near 33% (Astra 7x Sol's cost); Grok 4.7 29%; Haiku 5.5 and Luna under $0.50 per rollout and lowest pass (Results/Performance and compute)
Pooled over 10,095 rollouts: 28% pass, 66% right-call rate; 25 of 79 cases never passed by any rollout
Pass = right call AND reasoning score >= 0.8; no model reached half its rollouts at any threshold >= 0.6; between 42% and 66% of right calls still failed the reasoning check (Fig 2, Fig 5)

Scoring: gate (valid decision, judgment on every scenario, alerted counts/totals reconcile; else -1) -> call (missed escalation -1, over-escalation -0.25) -> reasons = 0.8 x counterparties + 0.2 x scenarios; counterparties matched by exact alerted count and total, credit for relationship and suspicious flag, halved if full-period totals wrong, weighted by alerted dollars

Dataset: 79 cases; 34 escalate / 45 dismiss; 38 business (16 esc/22 dis), 41 personal (18/23); counterparties per case 1: 21? buckets listed 1, 2-3, 4-9, 10+ with counts 2,18,25,25 as flattened (text says about a quarter single counterparty, nearly a third 10+); 14 alert types

More reasoning helped little: Opus/Sonnet/Haiku/Sol/Astra used 8-21x reasoning tokens at highest vs lowest level for -1 to +5 points; Grok +3; Gemini 4 Argon +9 (low to high); Muse Wonder +8; Luna gain only from fewer unanswered rollouts
Of 651 wrong calls at best configs: a missed/misread row decided 2, wrong grouping 14, wrong role 66; judgment decided 80% of wrong calls for all but Haiku and Luna
Six of nine models lean lenient (cleared a red flag the analyst escalated); Luna and Muse lean strict (flagged benign: 56% and 49% of their wrong calls); Opus lenient in 70% of wrong calls

Lenient failure sub-types: stretching industry label, dismissing elder-abuse signs one at a time, taking counterparty legitimacy as proof of fit, clearing unknown-source funds because onward use looks ordinary, inventing an undocumented benign story (Opus 20%), dismissing trafficking keyword/third-party control

Strict failure sub-types: demanding proof for own-account money, escalating fitting supplier for missing invoice, lawful spending read as suspicious, self-funded loads/family remittances read as pass-through, ledger field quirks read as red flags

Right-call record quality: excluding Haiku and Luna, 1.0 split parties and 0.9 wrongly cleared parties per review; every model cleared parties the analyst left open (0.58-1.11 per review); 1,576 of 11,159 errors (14%) excluded as grader artifacts/analyst-reference inconsistencies
Matching counterparties = 64% of reasoning score lost on right calls (grouping rows into parties, not labeling)
Consistency: mean pairwise per-case accuracy correlation 0.56; three rollouts of a config agree on decision on 79% of cases; Argon failed all 3 on 40 of 79 cases and passed all 3 on 28
Difficulty by counterparty count: pass ~45% for 1-3 counterparties vs ~12% for 10+
Sample case: at each model's best level all 21 rollouts from seven models dismissed the 81-year-old's case; only one Haiku and one Luna rollout escalated (27 rollouts per model)

Takeaway: no model ready to resolve alerts without review; failures are consistent so can be measured, governed, trained against; vendor argues for training on verifier-dense reward rather than prompting

Public AML datasets (IBM AMLworld, AMLSim, SAML-D) contain shortcuts (date cutoff, amount threshold) recovering much of label; no public source joins transactions, customer records and analyst outcomes because of SAR confidentiality

key_results: STATUS: consultation paper, not adopted. Published Frankfurt 3 June 2026; responses by 03.09.2026; 'final guidelines, that will be issued in Q4 2026' (s2.1, p.5). Level-3 guidelines under Art. 26(5) AMLR mandate. Addressed to obliged entities and supervisors (para 2); competent authorities should consider them when assessing effectiveness of monitoring (s3.3 table).

Core principles: risk-based approach, proportionality, horizontal applicability to financial and non-financial sectors, technological neutrality (s3.2; IA/CBA overarching principles). Principle-based (Option B) chosen over prescriptive; AMLA wants outcomes not 'tick-the-box' compliance.

Technological neutrality (s3.2 p.8): 'The Guidelines do not prescribe the use of certain tools and do not mandate the use of automated systems'; automated and advanced analytical tools, 'including AI, should be considered where they enhance the identification and escalation of ML/TF risks. Their use is neither mandatory nor, in itself, an indicator of effectiveness'; entities must 'be able to explain their role and outputs to competent authorities, including where third-party providers are relied upon'.

Para 87 (2.11): assess whether 'automated or advanced analytical tools, including algorithms, machine learning, artificial intelligence and other innovative technologies' would enhance identification and escalation; consider whether manual processes suffice given risk exposure, complexity, size, volume and speed. 'The deployment of such tools should not, in itself, be considered an indicator of effectiveness'; effectiveness = detecting and escalating ML/TF risks 'without undue delay'.

Para 88-89: safeguards proportionate to size/nature/complexity/risk and the tool's impact on outcomes; outputs reviewable and challengeable; responsibility clearly assigned. Safeguards (oversight, challenge, explainability) commensurate with the tool's role; account for model risk: 'inaccuracies, biases, lack of robustness or limited transparency'; also the risk of 'delaying or limiting improvements in detection capabilities' and avoid 'unnecessary constraints' (anti-over-regulation counterweight).

Para 90: demonstrate and explain role, functioning and outputs to competent authorities 'in a manner that enables effective understanding, assessment and challenge of those outputs, without requiring full technical interpretability of the underlying model' (no full-interpretability mandate).

Para 91: third-party tools: if insufficient information available to meet the requirements, entities 'should not rely on such tools for monitoring functions that materially influence monitoring outcomes or decisions'.

Paras 92-93: data quality and integrity, attribution of data to customers/counterparties/assets; document material limitations and deficiencies in quality, accuracy, attribution, completeness plus mitigating measures.

Para 94: AI outputs 'should support monitoring decisions' and be subject to governance, oversight, challenge and control 'in a manner that avoids discriminatory outcomes'. Para 95: tools maintain expected performance over time, including detection of 'material performance degradation or drift'; entities remain responsible for decisions, which can be reviewed/adjusted incl. effective human oversight.

Para 44: monitoring must detect risks that emerge only when transactions are considered together over time: linked/repeated/aggregated behaviour across accounts, customers, devices, wallets or other identifiers; behavioural patterns over time; network relationships concealing ownership/control/economic purpose; structuring (value accumulated, split or transferred across multiple transactions). Para 39: for complex businesses analyse aggregated flows and activity patterns. Para 70: aggregated or behavioural analysis post-transaction for patterns, linkages, cumulative risk indicators.

Para 34: framework based on BWRA; leverages systems required by other law (TFR, PSR) and fraud/unusual-behaviour systems already existing (34a); complete, accurate, timely data incl. group information (34b); covers all products and services (34c); identifies material deviation from expected behaviour (34d); identifies TFS non-implementation/evasion patterns via intermediaries, ownership/control structures (34e); effective at implementation and over time via testing and adaptation (34f).

Paras 48-50: rules, scenarios, thresholds, models, behavioural baselines clearly defined; document, test and record updates to detection logic; pre-configured/vendor tools: understand their use, assess and calibrate default settings; 'Default settings should not be used without a documented assessment of their appropriateness'.

Paras 53-56: customer profiles based on verified CDD info (purpose, expected transactions, expected behavioural profile); baseline for deviation detection; peer/reference groups allowed but deviation from group pattern must be assessed against individual profile, 'absence of a deviation at peer-group level should not, on its own, be used to dismiss risk indicators identified at individual customer level' (para 54); peer groups not to be used where behaviour is inherently heterogeneous (55); keep profiles up to date regardless of periodic review due (56).

Paras 75-79 (alert handling): outputs assessed without undue delay, prioritised by risk, escalated to knowledgeable staff; manage backlog accumulation (76); objectivity/independence (77); automated closure only for cases that after automated analysis do not indicate suspicion, never where heightened-risk indicators or higher-risk customers (78); decision logic understood/documented, effectiveness subject to human oversight incl. 'periodic validation through sampling, the review of potential cases where suspicious transactions or activities were not identified' (79).

Paras 81-86 (testing and effectiveness): periodic review/testing of framework (81); data quality controls, validation, cleansing; testing 'should, where appropriate, rely on synthetic or anonymised data'; real personal data only if strictly necessary (82); define outcomes and reassess (83); para 84: effectiveness 'should not be assessed solely by reference to alert, reporting volumes or to the breadth of typology coverage'; consider timeliness of escalation, appropriateness of outcomes, recurring deficiencies; para 85: when materially changing monitoring logic or methods, apply documented transition and validation framework, 'testing that goes beyond comparison with legacy outputs' (no champion/challenger-only validation); 86: assigned responsibility, staff able to understand and challenge tools.

Para 45: be able to explain material changes in monitoring behaviour/outcomes from updates to rules, thresholds, models, analytical methods. Para 43: framework must absorb new typologies, red flags from supervisors/FIUs 'without undue delay'.

Monitoring timing definitions (def d-f, paras 58-73): pre-transaction (preventive, before execution; proceed/delay/escalate), real-time (at execution), post-transaction (patterns after the fact). Where entity can intervene before execution it should apply pre-transaction/real-time monitoring; legal/technical constraints cannot justify absence where entity is in a position to intervene (para 66). Default: continuous monitoring (58); staged monitoring only if justified and documented (59).

Ongoing monitoring is wider than transaction monitoring: 'transactions and activities', behaviours, events (para 4; s3.2). Periodic review max intervals set by Art.26(2) AMLR (five-year maximum cited in IA); event-driven review per Art.26(3); depth and intensity of periodic review risk-based (paras 19-20); trigger events list incl. unusual transaction patterns, repeated changes in IP address or device location, adverse media, PEP status (para 27).

Para 30-33: where customer info cannot be updated, entity shall refrain from transactions and terminate relationship (Arts 20, 21 AMLR); may temporarily suspend/restrict before termination if risks manageable; keep records (Art.21(3)).
Para 82 and 10: GDPR necessity and data minimisation apply to personal data used in monitoring and testing.

IA/CBA (s5.1): qualitative only, quantitative figures unavailable; three policy issues, each resolved: A horizontal structure, B principle-based, B risk-based re-collection of expired ID documents. Notes EBA/GL/2021/02 as prior financial-sector guidance and newly in-scope sectors (crowdfunding, football clubs/agents, investment migration, CASPs, high-value goods traders).

gems: Para 84 (p.39): effectiveness explicitly NOT to be judged solely by alert volumes, reporting volumes or typology breadth; timeliness of escalation, appropriateness of outcomes, recurring deficiencies instead. Good hook for evaluating fraud/AML models beyond alert counts.

Para 85 (pp.39-40): validation of a new monitoring approach must include 'testing that goes beyond comparison with legacy outputs' - regulator rejecting 'matches the old system' as validation; relevant to label/ground-truth scarcity.
Para 90 (pp.40-41): explicit statement that no 'full technical interpretability of the underlying model' is required, only explanation enabling effective understanding, assessment and challenge.
Para 54 (p.34): absence of peer-group deviation must not dismiss individual-level risk indicators - a precise statement about peer-group baselines vs individual baselines.

Para 44d (p.32): individually low-risk transactions forming concerning patterns when value is accumulated, split, or transferred across multiple transactions (structuring) - regulatory phrasing of why per-transaction rules are insufficient; 44a lists devices and wallets as linking identifiers.

Para 78-79 (p.38): automated alert closure allowed only for cases with no indicators and never for higher-risk customers; effectiveness checked by sampling of potential missed cases (false-negative review).
Para 95 (p.41): regulator names 'performance degradation or drift' monitoring as an expectation for AI tools.
Para 89 (p.40): two-sided stance: model risk (bias, robustness, opacity) but also warns against delaying detection improvements through unnecessary constraints.
Para 50 (p.33): vendor default settings may not be used without documented appropriateness assessment.
Para 82 (p.39): testing on synthetic or anonymised data for functional validation; real personal data only if strictly necessary.
Para 27b (p.26): repeated or unusual changes in IP address or device location listed as a trigger for customer review.
IA/CBA policy issue 3 (pp.50-53): worked option appraisal on whether expired ID documents are automatically re-collected - chose risk-based; illustrates principle-based vs prescriptive trade-off.
Para 34a (p.29): existing fraud/unusual-behaviour detection systems and TFR/PSR transaction-monitoring systems should be leveraged for AML monitoring (links fraud and AML tooling).
figures: None: the document has no figures or diagrams. The only structured visual is the table in s3.3 (p.9-10) mapping other L1/2/3 instruments to relevance for ongoing monitoring, and the structure of Guideline 1 vs Guideline 2 in s3.4. A lesson could recreate a map of 'where AI/analytics are addressed' across paras 28, 34, 44, 48-50, 78-79, 85, 87-95, or a timeline pre-transaction / real-time / post-transaction.
pedagogy: Regulatory consultation paper, not a textbook. Numbered paragraphs 1-95 in 'should' language (supervisory expectations, Level 3 guidelines), framed by background/rationale (s3) and a qualitative impact assessment (s5.1). No proofs, no worked numeric examples, no exercises; consultation questions Q1-Q7 (s5.2) are the only prompts. Assumes familiarity with AMLR (Regulation 2024/1624) articles 19, 20, 21, 26, 28, 69, business-wide risk assessment, CDD, SARs, TFS, GDPR. Very principle-based and deliberately non-prescriptive: no thresholds, metrics, model families or validation procedures named; AI is covered only through generic safeguards (proportionality, explainability, oversight, drift, bias, third-party reliance). Useful as the regulatory frame and exact-wording source, not as technical content.

key_results: FATF: Deepfake definition (p.3 and fn.1): synthetic audio-visual media made with deep learning to mimic real people; no universally accepted definition; barrier to entry now a smartphone and minutes.
FATF: Deepfakes attack CDD (Recs 10 and 22 require 'reliable documents, data or information from independent sources'); biometric/video KYC is the main attack surface (pp.3-4).
FATF: Three risk amplifiers (p.4): reliance on biometric verification; persistent lag in AML tech adoption; cross-border complexity of remote ID.

FATF: Dual-use multiplier effect (Box 0.1, pp.4-5): low-skilled actors use off-the-shelf tools; skilled actors replicate fingerprints, browser behaviour and credentials, infostealer malware to defeat 2FA; slopsquatting-style package hallucination attacks.
FATF: Hybrid synthetic identities merge victim and suspect data to open accounts and pass facial recognition (Box 0.2, p.5).

FATF: Countermeasure stack (pp.5-8): hardware-backed, passive plus active liveness detection; multi-factor auth; AI-driven KYC detection; deepfake detection software; blockchain analytics; human expertise for anomalies automated systems miss.

FATF: FIU behavioural indicators (p.8): coordinated activity, rapid transactions to newly opened accounts, immediate withdrawals after deposits, IP/profile mismatch, same device used by different counterparts, unusually high volumes, elevated chargebacks and rejected payments.
FATF: Detection techniques go obsolete quickly; partnerships are the answer (p.8).

FATF: Taxonomy of AI threat by deployment style (p.10): discriminative/predictive, generative, agents, theoretical General AI. Footnote 7: predictive models used in AML/fraud (risk scoring, SAR prediction, anomaly detection) give attackers incentive to target them.

FATF: Algorithmic pattern mimicry (p.10): ML trained on normal transaction data (payroll, trade payments) generates synthetic transaction sequences that statistically resemble genuine activity, evading monitoring.
FATF: Adversarial AI learns red flags from typology reports and guidance and evades them (p.12).

FATF: Footnote 9 (p.11) lists defensive approaches: graph/network analytics, real-time ML monitoring with anomaly detection, adaptive customer profiling, consortium intelligence, adversarial-robust ML with continuous red-teaming, human-in-the-loop review, synthetic-data testing of agent behaviours, explainable AI governance.
FATF: Black-box AI outputs weaken evidentiary value; volume of synthetic evidence strains chain of custody (p.12).
FATF: No consistent enforceable global AI regulation; FATF Rec 15 covers new technologies (pp.13-14).

FinCEN: Deepfake definition (fn 2, p1): synthetic content using AI/ML to create realistic but inauthentic video, pictures, audio, text; per DHS the threat comes from people's inclination to believe what they see, so deepfakes need not be advanced to work.
FinCEN: GenAI greatly reduces resources to produce high-quality synthetic content; open-source tools let users modify code and circumvent controls (p2).

FinCEN: Main observed attack: GenAI-altered or generated ID images (driver's licences, passport cards/books) to defeat CIP/CDD identity verification; combined with stolen or fake PII to form synthetic identities (p2-3, fn 14 definition of synthetic identity).

FinCEN: Resulting accounts are used to receive and launder proceeds of other fraud: check fraud, credit card fraud, authorized push payment fraud, loan fraud, unemployment fraud; also as funnel accounts (p3, fn 15 and 18 definitions).

FinCEN: Detection in practice (p3-4): mostly via re-review of account-opening documents; reverse image search matching online galleries of GenAI faces; metadata inspection; deepfake-detection software. Indicators are 'not conclusive'.
FinCEN: Document-level indicators (p4): inconsistencies among multiple ID documents; inability to authenticate identity or source of income; ID inconsistent with rest of profile.

FinCEN: Behavioural indicators warranting EDD (p4): IP inconsistent with profile; coordinated activity among similar accounts; high payments to gambling sites/digital asset exchanges; high chargebacks or rejected payments; rapid transactions from new or thin-history account; withdrawal right after deposit by hard-to-reverse routes (international wires, offshore exchanges).

FinCEN: Mitigations (p4-5): MFA incl. phishing-resistant MFA; live audio/video verification, noting actors may answer with synthetic audio/video, claim technical glitches or ask to switch channel; flag third-party webcam plugins that inject pre-generated video.

FinCEN: Nine red flags (p5-6): internally inconsistent photo or photo/DOB mismatch; inconsistent multiple IDs; third-party webcam plugin or channel switching in live check; declines MFA; reverse-image match to GenAI face gallery; photo/video flagged by deepfake detector; GenAI-text detector flags profile/responses; geo or device data inconsistent with ID; new/thin account with rapid transactions, risky payees, chargebacks. 'No single red flag is necessarily indicative'; judge on surrounding facts.
FinCEN: Reporting (p1, p6): include key term FIN-2024-DEEPFAKEFRAUD in SAR field 2 and narrative, plus typology key terms.

Ideas to recreate: a diagram of the three deepfake amplifiers hitting the CDD pipeline; an attacker-skill-tier vs tool diagram; a taxonomy table of discriminative/generative/agent/general AI against the fraud-model attack each enables; a pipeline sketch of the Scenario 3 mule-network automation.

gems: FATF Box 0.2 Case 1 (p.5): deepfake video conference impersonating senior executives of a multinational advisory firm; CFO instructed to transfer USD 25 million; part frozen.

FATF Box 0.3 (p.7): deepfake news broadcast with real anchors announcing a fake IPO; funds to a central account then unhosted wallets onboarded with deepfaked CDD; wallet provider itself under foreign sanctions.

FATF Box 0.5 (p.13): transaction monitoring flags odd volumes/timings/amounts; FI asks for premises photos; anti-counterfeiting plus big-data analysis matches storefront background to a prior counterfeit from a high-risk customer. Neat monitoring-to-verification hand-off story.
FATF Pattern mimicry (p.10): train on legitimate payroll/trade streams to generate laundering sequences that blend in; direct link to why supervised fraud models face adversarial drift.
FATF Package-hallucination typosquatting (Box 0.1, p.5): attackers register package names AI assistants repeatedly invent.
FATF Scenario 3 (p.11): agents run hundreds of mule accounts laundering millions USD per month via gaming/gambling platforms while deepfakes beat digital ID checks.
FATF Scenario 4 (p.12): LLM + retrieval over legal texts + jurisdiction/corporate knowledge graph + planning agents ranking sanctions-evasion routes.
FATF Adversarial AI trained on published typology reports and mutual evaluation reports (p.12): public guidance as attacker training data.

FinCEN attacker's evasion playbook against liveness checks (p4-5): claim repeated technical glitches, ask to switch communication channel, use a third-party webcam plugin to feed pre-generated video. Good set piece for an adversarial-adaptation lesson: each control induces a measurable counter-behaviour that becomes a feature.

FinCEN red-flag list (p5-6) maps almost one-to-one onto model features: photo/DOB age mismatch, device/geo vs ID mismatch, thin-history account with rapid transactions, chargeback rate, cash-out via irreversible channels.

FinCEN deepfake-enabled executive impersonation: fn 26 cites a finance worker paying out $25 million after a video call with a deepfake 'chief financial officer' (CNN, Feb 2024); same incident as FATF Box 0.2 Case 1.

FinCEN downstream view (p3): the deepfake ID is the entry ticket; the harm shows up as mule/funnel accounts receiving proceeds of APP, check, card, loan, unemployment fraud, so detection can happen at onboarding or from transaction behaviour.
FinCEN DHS quote (fn 2): deepfakes need not be sophisticated to be effective; the vulnerability is human belief.
FinCEN operational detail: SAR key term FIN-2024-DEEPFAKEFRAUD makes this typology searchable in BSA data, an example of labelling regime for supervised learning.
pedagogy: Two regulator documents, not textbooks: no proofs, no exercises, no quantitative evidence or data. The FATF horizon scan (15 pp.) is narrative plus boxed case studies from unnamed jurisdictions and agencies and hypothetical known-unknown scenarios; the FinCEN alert (6 pp.) is a compact typology note with dense footnotes (DHS, NSA/FBI/CISA, Treasury) and a nine-item red-flag list. Both assume AML/CFT vocabulary (CDD, KYC, CIP, SAR, FIU, VASP, DNFBP) and FATF Recommendations 10, 15, 22. Best used as authoritative citations for adversary capability claims and for qualitative detection indicators that translate into model features, not for technical detail; countermeasures are listed, not evaluated. The two overlap on the USD 25M deepfake video-call case and the behavioural indicators (rapid transactions on new accounts, chargebacks, IP mismatch).

key_results: Click-through (link pressed) by randomized arm, n=101: control 12% (n=26; 11.5% in Table 4), human expert 54% (n=24), fully AI 54% (n=26), AI + human-in-the-loop 56% (n=25) -> AI is about 350% better than control and on par with experts (Abstract, Sec 5.1, Fig 5)
Only 60 of 101 participants showed any activity (claimed gift card or got phished), so true phished rate may be higher (Sec 5.1)

OSINT agent quality: 88% level 3 (correct, sufficient), 8% level 2, 4% level 1 (wrong person); content: 71% needed no change, 25% minor language, 4% structural (Table 3). 2023 comparison: 25% no change, 50% level 2, 25% level 1

Human intervention: 8% of OSINT, 48% of texts touched, 75% of those minor; 1 min to check even when unchanged; 2:41 min average edit time; manual replication of OSINT+email 34 min per target (23:27 + 10:10); HITL about 92% faster; fully automated about 4 cents per email (Sec 5.1.1)

Detection: priming for suspicion ('is this suspicious' vs 'what is the intent') raises detection without raising false positives; Claude 3.5 Sonnet 97.25% true-positive on 363 phishing emails, 0 false positives on 18 legitimate (category-weighted 97.64%); worst on conventional 'Phishing' category (81%), 100% on Expert emails; GPT-4o clearly worse; Mistral had many false positives when primed (Sec 4, 5.2, Figs 7-8)
Safety guardrails bypassed by simple rephrasing ('phishing email' -> 'email') and resampling; recon agent never refused, guardrails weaker in agent settings (Sec 3.1, 3.6)
Economic model: revenue r_j(t,X_i)=m(X_i) p_j(t,X_i) q; cost c(t)=w t - C (as printed); phish iff max_t E[(r-c)/t] >= 0 (Sec 6.1)

Calibration: payoff $136 per successful phish; q = 0.6%/2.35%/7.9% (low/median/high conversion rates from marketing); wages US $34.55/h vs Russia $5.47/h; fixed cost 1 cent per email (domains) plus 4 cents for AI; times 15/30/1/4:24 min (Sec 6.2, Table 4)

Table 4 profit/hour: control negative everywhere (about -$34 to -$0.6); human expert positive only at high q abroad ($6.1); AI fully automated +$65.7 (med q, home) to $338.6 (high q, abroad); hybrid $7.4 to $137.9. Pure AI beats hybrid: value of human skill reverses once AI is an option

Break-even including sunk dev cost (260 h x $62 = $16,120): group size 2,859 (high q), 10,213 (med q), 54,123 (low q); about 5,000 targets AI beats human expert at any q; up to 50x profitability for large audiences (Sec 6.2, Fig 9)
Semi-personalized expert email scales to small groups (one email for 25) but not to large diverse audiences; expert cost grows linearly (Sec 3.5.2, 5.1)
Free-text reasons: about 40% of both AI groups cited personalization as trust driver vs 0% control and about 20% expert; sender was the top suspicion indicator (spoofed domain) (Sec 5.1, Fig 6)
Conclusion: signature-based spam filters are obsolete against per-target unique LLM text; AI vs AI detection future; defenders can reuse vulnerability profiles and footprint reduction (Sec 7.1, 8)
Linear projection of AI performance relative to expert: 2023 43%, 2024 about 99-103%, 2025 projected about 144-155% (Fig 12, A.7; crude 3-point extrapolation)

pedagogy: Empirical security paper, not a textbook: no proofs; one stylized economic model with calibrated parameters; brief power-analysis explanation in lay terms; significance stars on Table 4 (two-sided t-tests relative to control). Assumes basic phishing/OSINT vocabulary and LLM familiarity; no code or exercises. Prompts withheld for safety. Small-sample, convenience-population study with dual-use framing; authors are candid that numbers are short-run and likely overestimate profit (conversion time excluded).
